Microbiology Spectrum.title: Evaluation of point-of-care testing (POCT) for blood-borne infections in forensic autopsy specimens.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA)-based point-of-care testing (POCT) for viral antigen and antibody detection enables rapid screening for blood-borne viral infections and may be particularly valuable in forensic autopsy settings, where incomplete antemortem medical histories and invasive procedures increase the risk of occupational exposure. However, its performance in postmortem specimens remains unclear. We evaluated the applicability of LFIA-based POCT for detecting human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and hepatitis B virus (HBV) in autopsy specimens, focusing on postmortem decomposition and the use of solid organ tissues as alternatives to blood. A total of 309 cases were analyzed using LFIA and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) across blood, liver, and spleen specimens. Agreement was assessed using overall, positive, and negative percent agreement and Cohen's kappa coefficient (κ). Positivity rates were compared by specimen type and decomposition status. LFIA agreement with qPCR varied by marker and specimen type, with substantial agreement for HIV and HCV antibody detection in blood and lower agreement in liver and spleen. Fresh specimens generally demonstrated higher LFIA positivity rates than decomposed specimens. Among specimens meeting predefined qPCR positivity criteria, LFIA-positive specimens tended to exhibit higher viral loads than LFIA-negative specimens, reaching statistical significance for HBV in liver, with similar but non-significant trends for blood HBV and liver HCV. LFIA-based POCT may serve as a preliminary screening tool in postmortem settings, particularly when blood is available. Nevertheless, negative results do not exclude infection-especially with low viral loads or advanced decomposition-and should be confirmed by molecular testing.IMPORTANCEForensic personnel performing autopsies face significant occupational risks from exposure to blood-borne viruses, including human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C virus. Unlike clinical settings, forensic autopsies frequently involve bodies with unknown infection histories, making rapid infection screening essential for personnel safety. Lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA)-based point-of-care testing (POCT) for viral antigen and antibody detection offers a rapid, infrastructure-free screening option; however, its performance in postmortem specimens has not been systematically evaluated. This study suggests that rapid immunochromatographic POCT may serve as a preliminary screening tool in forensic autopsy settings, particularly when blood specimens are available. However, a negative result does not exclude infection, especially in cases with low viral load or advanced decomposition, and confirmatory molecular testing remains necessary. These findings provide practical guidance for forensic professionals on appropriate specimen selection and interpretation of LFIA results, ultimately supporting safer autopsy practices.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Gentamicin treatment in a murine infection model suggests extracellular Orientia tsutsugamushi contributes to systemic dissemination.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular bacterial pathogen, infects multiple cell types and disseminates via the blood and lymphatic system to affect various organs in human and other mammalian hosts. This bacterium replicates exclusively within living cells; however, it also exists transiently in a metabolically inactive extracellular form. While infected leukocytes are known contributors to the systemic spread of the bacterium, the role of the inactive extracellular form in dissemination has been unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that extracellular bacteria are present in the cell-free plasma fraction of infected human and murine blood. Furthermore, treatment with gentamicin, a membrane-impermeable antibiotic, significantly reduces systemic bacterial growth in a murine infection model. These findings suggest a potential role for the extracellular form of the bacterium in the spread of infection and raise the possibility of exploring the use of gentamicin to augment conventional antibiotic therapy during scrub typhus infection.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: In vitro efficacy of synthetic antimicrobial peptide SET-M33 against poultry isolates with diverse antimicrobial resistance phenotypes.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Antimicrobial resistance is an impactful One Health issue. One of its drivers is the extensive use of antibiotics in both human and animal production systems, and despite regulatory restrictions on antibiotic use in poultry farming, antimicrobial resistance remains a major challenge. Consequently, animals are at higher risk of harder-to-treat diseases and play a role as resistance reservoirs, highlighting the need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. Toward this end, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising candidates due to their broad-spectrum activity and lower propensity to induce resistance. However, the effectiveness of AMPs against poultry pathogens, and in particular multidrug-resistant strains, is largely unclear. Here, we evaluated SET-M33, a synthetic tetrabranched AMP, against four species of clinically relevant pathogens in poultry, namely, Escherichia coli, Salmonella enterica, Enterococcus faecalis, and Enterococcus cecorum. Using a panel of 141 field isolates, we found that SET-M33 broadly inhibited bacterial growth at low micromolar concentrations (median minimum inhibitory concentrations of 2.5 and 5 μM for gram-negative and gram-positive strains, respectively), including in multidrug-resistant isolates. To examine the potential impact of SET-M33 on host cells, we established an in vitro co-cultivation system using chicken intestinal organoids. We found that SET-M33 retains its antimicrobial activity in organoid-microbe co-cultures at concentrations that preserve host cell viability. These findings demonstrate the potential of SET-M33 as a new antimicrobial agent against pathogens in poultry. [IMPORTANCE] Antimicrobial resistance is an important One Health issue that affects human and animal health. In particular, antimicrobial resistance remains a challenge in poultry farming, where animals are at a higher risk of harder-to-treat diseases and play a role as resistance reservoirs. To solve this issue, we need alternative antimicrobial strategies, and antimicrobial peptides have emerged as particularly promising candidates. Here, we examined the efficacy of one such new antimicrobial, the synthetic antimicrobial peptide SET-M33, against a large panel of poultry pathogen isolates. We found that SET-M33 was highly effective against the vast majority of isolates, including strains that are multidrug resistant or resistant to other antimicrobial peptides. To examine the potential impact of SET-M33 on the host, we established an in vitro co-cultivation system using chicken intestinal organoids. We found that SET-M33 retains its antimicrobial activity in organoid-microbe co-cultures at concentrations that preserve host cell viability.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: A dual-action combination therapy targeting bacteria and host immunity against bacterial infections.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance, coupled with a stagnant novel antibiotic discovery pipeline, underscores the urgent need for innovative strategies to combat bacterial infections. The development of antibiotic adjuvants that increase the efficacy of existing drugs represents a critical approach for addressing this challenge. We demonstrate that combining the conventional antibiotic azithromycin with the quorum-sensing inhibitor norharmane exerts potent antibacterial effects through both direct bactericidal activity and host immune activation. This combination not only disrupts bacterial structural integrity but also promotes macrophage polarization toward the M1-type phenotype and upregulates the expression of the important mediator, Muc5b, through activation of the IL-17 signaling pathway, ultimately enhancing mucosal immune defense and tissue repair functions. This regimen shows potent antibacterial efficacy against a range of pathogens in vitro and in vivo, along with a favorable safety profile. These findings highlight a promising combinatorial therapeutic strategy against the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. [IMPORTANCE] Antibiotic resistance has become one of the most urgent threats to global public health, yet the development of new antibiotics has slowed dramatically. In this study, we propose a promising alternative strategy that combines azithromycin with a small-molecule compound capable of inhibiting bacterial quorum sensing. This combination not only kills bacteria more effectively than the antibiotic alone but also harnesses the body's own immune system to fight infection. Its mechanisms of action include disrupting bacterial structure, promoting the polarization of macrophages toward the M1-type phenotype, and enhancing bactericidal capacity by activating the IL-17 signaling pathway to stimulate the production of the Muc5b protein. Our findings suggest that this dual-pronged approach could help revitalize existing antibiotics, offering a practical pathway to combat drug-resistant infections.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Distinct cell-type-specific gene expression programs associated with persistence versus clearance of arterivirus infection.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: This study aims to identify cellular markers correlated to persistent viral infection by a comprehensive comparison of blood immune transcriptomes and cell composition from acute and long-term stages of infection using a porcine arterivirus as the model. We applied single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to characterize blood mononuclear cells collected at 14 (acute) and 84 (long-term) days post-infection (DPI) with porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV). Pigs were grouped as persistently infected (PI, n = 5 at 14 DPI; n = 10 at 84 DPI) or virus-extinct (VE, n = 2) phenotypes based on detection of viral RNA in blood collected weekly and tissue samples collected at either 14 or 84 DPI. Monocytes emerged as the primary cellular drivers of infection outcome, with divergence driven mainly by cell-type-specific transcriptional programs rather than differences in immune cell compositions. At 14 DPI, genes expressed at higher levels in monocytes from VE pigs, which were enriched for activation of antiviral and interferon responses, and subsequently transitioned toward a homeostatic profile by 84 DPI. In contrast, monocytes from PI pigs were characterized by metabolic dysregulation at 14 DPI, followed by a chronic inflammation profile at 84 DPI. Temporal analysis revealed the "when and how" rather than the intensity of immune activation as a critical determinant of outcome, with PI pigs failing to mount early, effective antiviral responses. Collectively, these findings identified early monocyte transcriptional programs associated with PRRSV persistence, offering a potential application in the selection of biomarkers for disease surveillance and outbreak management in swine production.IMPORTANCEPersistent viral infection remains a critical challenge in human health, as well as livestock disease management, yet the viral-host immune mechanisms that determine whether infection resolves or persists remain poorly understood. This study used a swine arterivirus persistent infection model system along with advanced single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technology to address a broad biological significance question-how circulating immune cell-type-specific transcriptional programs at early stages of infection determine long-term viral outcomes in the host. This work generated the first scRNA-seq data set for porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) persistent infection and provides a framework for mining cell-type-resolved blood transcriptomes, which could assist in developing therapeutic strategies to manipulate host immune responses toward viral extinction pathways during infection.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Identification of a small molecule that inhibits Pks13 with anti-tuberculosis activity.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The persistent spread of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) necessitates the development of novel anti-TB agents characterized by high efficacy and innovative mechanisms of action. Polyketide synthase 13 (Pks13), a vital protein in the mycolic acid biosynthetic pathway, serves as a valuable target for TB therapy due to its exclusive presence in the genus Mycobacterium. This study identified a compound, B-AP15, that potently inhibited the activity of the Pks13 thioesterase domain (Pks13-TE), giving an IC50 of 22.48 μM. The binding interaction between B-AP15 and Pks13-TE was corroborated via surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis and molecular docking. Furthermore, site-directed mutagenesis, SPR analysis, and inhibitory activity assays of mutant enzymes revealed that residues H1664 and Q1633 likely serve as key binding residues for the interaction between B-AP15 and Pks13-TE. Additionally, B-AP15 exerted an inhibitory effect on Mycobacterium tuberculosis and potential intracellular anti-TB efficacy in macrophages similar to that of first-line anti-TB drugs. The higher minimum inhibitory concentration of B-AP15 for M. marinum strain overexpressing Pks13 confirmed that Pks13 is likely the target of this compound. Collectively, this study identified a Pks13 inhibitor, B-AP15, which exhibits considerable potential as a lead compound for anti-TB therapy. [IMPORTANCE] The spread of drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) urgently requires new anti-TB drugs with novel mechanisms. Pks13, a key enzyme in the mycolic acid biosynthetic pathway, is an attractive therapeutic target. We identified B-AP15 as a potent Pks13 inhibitor with a distinct scaffold from previously reported Pks13 inhibitors. B-AP15 directly binds Pks13 and exhibits in vitro and intracellular anti-TB activity comparable to first-line anti-TB drugs, with promising activity especially against drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This study provides a promising lead compound for developing anti-TB agents.

Genome Research.title: Base composition reflects RNA polymerase II displacement.
Genome Research.abstract: RNA polymerase II (Pol II) transcribes all protein-coding and many non-protein-coding genes in the genome. Pol II transcription termination is crucial for RNA maturation and, when disrupted, can lead to altered RNA processing and RNA export. Termination involves two intertwined processes: RNA cleavage and Pol II release from the DNA (displacement). Despite its importance, the exact mechanisms underlying Pol II displacement from the DNA remain poorly understood. Moreover, under certain cellular stress conditions, there is a partial failure of cleavage, leading to a shift of the position of displacement further downstream, a phenomenon known as readthrough transcription. We present a systematic analysis of Pol II termination across cell types and species and provide novel insights into the mechanism of displacement. Using a probabilistic mixture model to quantify Pol II dynamics across entire gene bodies from nascent RNA sequencing data, we find that genes fall into two classes defined by conserved base composition patterns near the displacement site. Both classes share a T-rich region upstream of displacement, and one class additionally carries a GC-rich region surrounding displacement. We find that GC-rich predisplacement regions have more accessible chromatin and higher levels of phospho-threonine 4 on the CTD of Pol II. Additionally, we find that displacement at genes with only the upstream T-rich pattern are more likely to be affected by perturbations that alter displacement, including heat shock, viral infection, kinase inhibition, and arsenic treatment. Thus, our work identifies two types of Pol II displacement regions, which are differentially affected by perturbations of cellular homeostasis.

Genome Research.title: The Vizitig pangenome and pantranscriptome explorer.
Genome Research.abstract: Vizitig is the first platform for real-time exploration and querying of DNA and RNA sequence de Bruijn graphs across many samples, unifying visualization, metadata, and flexible search. It constructs compacted colored de Bruijn graphs from raw sequencing reads and reference sequences and then provides an interactive web interface for graph exploration. It integrates raw and reference-based data, handles complex variation, and provides a human-readable feature-based (also referred to as metadata) query language with scalable graph loading. Its domain-specific query language supports composable searches combining sequences of arbitrary size, genomic features such as gene or exon identifiers, and experimental factors such as sample identifiers or abundance thresholds. On-demand subgraph loading retrieves only regions of interest, enabling interactive exploration of large data sets in the graphical user interface without loading the entire graph into memory. We demonstrate Vizitig's capabilities through case studies in pantranscriptomics and pangenomics. In pantranscriptomics, we recover fusion transcript breakpoints on long and short reads. In pangenomics, we explore sequence variations across yeast, rice, nematode, and human pangenomes. Vizitig scales from small virus genomes to human-scale pangenomes (our largest experiment comprises up to 20 assembled human haplotypes, on a laptop). Vizitig enables fast, reproducible analysis in both pangenomics and pantranscriptomics while providing a deployable and user-friendly working environment.

Genome Research.title: Liver X receptors participate in the fasting response by assisting CEBPB binding to enhancers and promoting the fasting transcriptional program.
Genome Research.abstract: Upon fasting, a group of transcription factors (TFs) activates an extensive transcriptional program in the liver to alter hepatocyte metabolism and cope with fasting. This is achieved by TF-mediated activation of enhancers, which become more accessible, leading to gene induction. Nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group H member 3 (NR1H3, also known as liver X receptor-alpha) and 2 (NR1H2, also known as liver X receptor-beta), collectively termed here LXRs, are important TFs known to participate in transcriptional programs in the fed state, but their role in fasting is unclear. Here, we examine the effect of LXR deletion on the transcriptional and chromatin programs activated in the fasted and fed states. We profile the liver transcriptome and genome-wide chromatin accessibility in single-knockout mice lacking either LXR isoform and in double-knockout mice lacking both isoforms. We find that double-knockout of LXRs impairs fasting-induced genes and enhancers. Analysis of genome-wide NR1H3 binding by ChIP-seq, together with chromatin accessibility profiling by ATAC-seq, shows that NR1H3 directly binds enhancers and increases their accessibility. We find that LXRs assist the binding of CCAAT enhancer binding protein beta (CEBPB) to enhancers during fasting. CEBPB is a key TF regulating the fasting response, and its genome-wide binding is perturbed in the absence of LXRs. Cooperation between LXRs and CEBPB promotes fasting-dependent gene induction. These findings reveal a previously unknown role for LXRs in the fasting response, whereby LXRs bind and increase enhancer accessibility, assist CEBPB binding, and promote gene induction. This study demonstrates the complex cooperation of TFs in regulating gene expression to maintain homeostasis during fasting and places LXRs as novel regulators of the fasting response.

Genome Research.title: Single-cell transcriptome analysis reveals onco-fetal reprogramming with implications for drug resistance and clinical outcome.
Genome Research.abstract: Onco-fetal (OF) reprogramming of the tumor ecosystem induces fetal-like characteristics, leading to tumor growth and malignant progression. Here, we develop a robust computational pipeline to systematically identify OF cells, using single-cell transcriptomic data from corresponding fetal and tumor tissues across multiple cancer types. OF cells are consistently detected across diverse malignancies and exhibit pronounced stem-like properties. Core transcription factors involved in OF reprogramming are identified, including PTMA, ATF5, TCF4, and FOS, whose coordinated activities may promote tumor progression. Strategically positioned OF cells orchestrate tumor microenvironment cross talk, specifically impairing B cell function. OF cells are further verified in additional cancers, and we find that high OF cell abundance contributes to enhanced drug resistance and cancer recurrence. Critically, pancancer analyses establish that OF cell markers universally portend adverse prognoses. Overall, our study uncovers a clinically consequential cancer cell subpopulation and highlights its potential as a target for precision oncology.

Genome Research.title: Shared transcriptional consequences of epigenetic machinery disruption in murine neuronal progenitors.
Genome Research.abstract: The Mendelian disorders of the epigenetic machinery (MDEMs) are an emerging group of disorders that commonly involve disruption of intellect and growth. To investigate consequences of epigenetic machinery (EM) disruption during neurodevelopment, we systematically knocked out (KO) EM factors in neuronal progenitors isolated from the murine hippocampus and established a neurodifferentiation model to interrogate their functions. We then profile gene expression and DNA methylation (DNAm) in the EM-KOs using RNA sequencing and Nanopore long-read DNA sequencing. Although Dnmt1-KO induces extensive DNAm alterations, Kmt2a-KO has little effect on methylation. Nevertheless, the disruption of Kmt2a and Dnmt1 produces convergent transcriptional changes. Loss of either EM factor leads to premature neuronal differentiation, partially explaining this convergence, and MYC emerges as a shared regulatory node linked to the downregulation of cell-cycle programs in these cells. Extending our methylation analysis to 46 EM genes, we find that loss of DNA methyltransferases induces the strongest DNAm changes, whereas other EM-KOs have subtle or negligible effects. However, clustering of EM-KOs based on promoter DNAm levels reveals three distinct EM subgroups, of which two are enriched for interactions with the DNAm machinery. Allele-specific analysis of DNAm further identifies a single differentially methylated region shared across the 46 EM-KOs, localized to the B6J allele over the Zic4 3' UTR. Furthermore, Zic4 overexpression appears to maintain the neuronal progenitor state, suggesting functional relevance of this locus. Taken together, our results reveal both gene-specific and convergent transcriptional effects across diverse EM-KOs and provide novel insights into the downstream consequences of EM dysfunction.

Most loci contain GGAA microsatellites bound by the tumor-defining EWSR1::FLI1 fusion protein, highlighting interplay between inherited genetic variation and somatically acquired oncogenic fusions in Ewing sarcoma.

Trends in Ecology & Evolution.title: The development of individuality: beyond nature and nurture
Trends in Ecology & Evolution.abstract: How does behavioral individuality arise? Theoretical models have highlighted the potential roles of genes and the environment. However, Gallagher et al. show that behavioral individuality occurs in the absence of genetic variation and is unaffected by experimentally manipulating the developmental environment. This suggests that behavioral individuality may originate even before birth.

EMBO Reports.title: An ATM-PPM1D circuit controls the processing and restart of DNA replication forks.
EMBO Reports.abstract: In response to DNA replication stress, DNA damage signaling kinases inhibit origin firing, stabilize replication forks, and reduce DNA synthesis to preserve genomic integrity, yet the mechanisms governing replication stress recovery, particularly stalled fork restart, remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the oncogenic phosphatase PPM1D/WIP1 as a regulator of replication fork restart. During recovery from replication stress, PPM1D prevents excessive MRE11- and DNA2-dependent nucleolytic degradation of stalled forks. Loss of PPM1D function leads to defects in RAD51 recruitment to chromatin and impairs RAD51-dependent fork restart. Phosphoproteomic analysis reveals that PPM1D regulates a network of ATM substrates, several of which are phosphorylated at an S/T-Q-(E/D)n motif. Strikingly, ATM inhibition suppresses the deleterious effects of PPM1D loss at replication forks, enabling timely fork restart. The dominant effect of ATM hyper-signaling in suppressing fork restart occurs, in part, through the excessive engagement of 53BP1 and consequent RAD51 antagonization. Together, these findings reveal a novel ATM signaling mode responding to fork stalling and establish PPM1D's role in restraining ATM signaling to facilitate proper fork restart.

EMBO Reports.title: Ubiquitin-dependent signal amplification in lipid saturation sensing.
EMBO Reports.abstract: Cellular membranes are dynamic platforms whose composition and biophysical properties are surveyed by sensor proteins to maintain homeostasis. Failure to preserve membrane homeostasis, however, results in cellular stress and organelle dysfunction. Using the prototypical lipid saturation sensor Mga2, we explored how weak physical cues that modulate rotational movements in the transmembrane region are converted into decisive biochemical outputs that ultimately control the production of unsaturated fatty acids. Using reconstituted systems and purified components, we quantitatively follow the ubiquitylation of Mga2 via the E3 ligase Rsp5. Kinetic modeling reveals that several rounds of ubiquitylation contribute to signal amplification and uncovers the first transfer of ubiquitin onto Mga2 as a kinetic gatekeeper. The minimal system composed of the sensor protein and a canonical E1-E2-E3 ubiquitylation cascade is sufficient to discriminate saturated and unsaturated membrane lipid environments even in the absence of deubiquitylating enzymes such as Ubp2. Our findings provide a mechanistic framework for how membrane property sensors convert weak, fluctuating physical cues into robust biochemical outcomes.

EMBO Reports.title: PI4K2A promotes cancer cell motility by regulating c-MET recycling.
EMBO Reports.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer mortality, largely due to metastatic disease. Cell surface proteins regulate tumor-stroma interactions and metastatic progression, and their abundance is dynamically controlled by secretion and endocytic recycling pathways. Using cancer cell surfaceome profiling, we identified phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase type 2α (PI4K2A) as a key regulator of cell surface protein levels. PI4K2A controls the membrane abundance and activity of receptor tyrosine kinases, including the c-MET proto-oncogene (MET), thereby promoting cancer cell motility - an early step in metastasis. Mechanistically, PI4K2A interacts with MET and directs endocytosed MET to RAB14-positive recycling endosomes, enhancing MET recycling and activation. Notably, this pro-recycling and pro-migratory function is independent of PI4K2A kinase activity and instead depends on its interaction with MET and RAB14 endosomes. These findings reveal a kinase-independent role for PI4K2A in regulating the cancer cell surfaceome.

Genome Biology.title: Spatial transcriptomics defines segmental and temporal dynamics of pig intestinal epithelium
Genome Biology.abstract: Background The pig (Sus scrofa) is widely studied as a large-animal model for human gastrointestinal biology, including gut physiology, pathology and disease. However, the spatial and developmental organisation of the pig intestine is not yet fully understood. Results Here, we generate a comprehensive spatiotemporal atlas of pig intestinal development by applying spatial transcriptomics to three intestinal segments across five developmental stages and an additional four intestinal segments at the adult stage. We identify spatial separation among enterocytes, plasma cells and stem cells, observing more pronounced separation in the small intestine compared to the large intestine. Pseudotime analysis of enterocyte-enriched regions reveals a gradient along the crypt-villus/crypt axis as early as post-conception day 70 in the jejunum, becoming fully evident across all intestinal segments by birth in the large intestine, with all three intestinal segments reaching a mature state by postnatal day 33. Our analysis indicates that the maturation of enterocytes during migration along the crypt-villus axis involves transcriptional programs similar to those governing enterocyte maturation across developmental stages, suggesting conserved molecular mechanisms governing both spatial and temporal differentiation. In the large intestine, nutrient transport-related gene expression declines progressively during development, transitioning from jejunum-like levels at early stages to markedly reduced levels in adulthood, consistent with functional specialization of distinct intestinal segments. Conclusions Our study provides a high-resolution spatiotemporal framework of pig intestinal development and establishes a valuable resource for comparative biology and translational research.

mSystems.title: Metal-independent effects of calprotectin on cocultures of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus involve alkylquinolone production.
mSystems.abstract: The current working model of the innate immune protein calprotectin (CP) focuses on its metal-sequestering activity, which contributes to host defense against infection. Recently, CP was reported to enhance the survival of Staphylococcus aureus in coculture with Pseudomonas aeruginosa in a metal-independent manner. This prior work indicated that the CP protein scaffold, even in the absence of its metal-binding sites, possesses activities that impact interspecies dynamics between these bacterial pathogens. In this study, we employ ΔΔ, a CP variant lacking both functional metal-binding sites, to investigate metal-independent activities of the CP protein scaffold. Using dual-species transcriptomics, we report that ΔΔ treatment induced gene expression changes indicative of cell envelope modifications for both P. aeruginosa and S. aureus during coculture. The presence of the CP protein scaffold also attenuated the production of the quorum sensing molecule C4-homoserine lactone and the anti-staphylococcal alkylquinolone (AQ) metabolite 2-heptyl-4-hydroxyquinoline N-oxide. Cocultures with S. aureus and P. aeruginosa mutants defective in AQ biosynthesis demonstrated that AQ production was required for ∆∆ to impact expression of membrane remodeling genes in both species during coculture. Furthermore, we showed that in the absence of AQ production, the effect of CP on S. aureus in coculture resembled that of Fe depletion. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that the functional versatility of CP extends beyond multi-metal sequestration and that its intertwined metal-dependent and -independent activities have important consequences for bacterial physiology and polymicrobial interactions.IMPORTANCERecent studies of the innate immune protein calprotectin (CP), which is known for its metal-sequestering ability and contributions to nutritional immunity, uncovered that the protein also exerts metal-independent activities on bacterial pathogens. In this work, we investigate the metal-independent effects of CP on the interspecies dynamics of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, two high-priority pathogens that co-colonize various polymicrobial infection sites. We report that the ability of the CP protein scaffold to attenuate the anti-staphylococcal activity of P. aeruginosa results from perturbed quorum sensing and reduced production of alkylquinolone (AQ) metabolites. We further show that pseudomonal AQs contribute to cell envelope remodeling responses exhibited by both pathogens in the presence of the CP protein scaffold. As such, this study is the first to interrogate the CP protein scaffold absent its metal-binding sites, demonstrating that both canonical metal-dependent and non-canonical metal-independent activities of CP elicit physiological changes that perturb coculture dynamics.

Journal of Virology.title: Fish TRAF6 shapes interferon antiviral response by targeting the background MAVS for protein degradation.
Journal of Virology.abstract: The interferon (IFN)-mediated antiviral immune response is tightly regulated to prevent insufficient or excessive immune activation. In mammals, the E3 ubiquitin ligase tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) is generally considered a positive regulator of IFN signaling although its role in fish may differ. In this study, zebrafish TRAF6 showed opposing regulatory effects on different retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptor (RLR) signaling components in overexpression assays, but knockdown and knockout experiments further supported its overall negative regulatory role in the fish IFN response. To investigate this inhibitory mechanism, we uncovered a previously unrecognized role of zebrafish TRAF6 in promoting the degradation of mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS) under basal conditions in an E3 ligase activity-dependent manner. Zebrafish TRAF6 bound to the N-terminal caspase recruitment domain (CARD) of MAVS in the cytoplasm and promoted lysosome-dependent MAVS degradation. Lys286 and Lys293 contributed to this degradation and were required for TRAF6-enhanced K48-linked polyubiquitination of MAVS. Simultaneous mutation of both residues increased basal MAVS protein levels and enhanced its ability to activate the IFN response. Our data also suggest that TRAF6 may promote MAVS degradation through a proteasome-dependent pathway involving the C-terminal region of MAVS. TRAF6 knockout (TRAF6-KO) zebrafish exhibited significantly enhanced resistance to spring viremia of carp virus (SVCV) infection. Basal MAVS protein levels were also significantly higher in TRAF6-KO tissues than in wild-type (WT) zebrafish. Collectively, our results reveal a critical role of zebrafish TRAF6 in regulating basal MAVS expression to fine-tune IFN-mediated antiviral innate immunity.IMPORTANCEInterferon (IFN)-mediated innate immunity is essential for protecting fish against viral infection, but excessive IFN activation can also be harmful to the host. Here, we identify zebrafish TRAF6 as a dual regulator of IFN-mediated antiviral signaling. In overexpression assays, TRAF6 enhanced RIG-I-mediated signaling and increased K63-linked ubiquitination of the RIG-I signaling complex while suppressing MAVS-mediated signaling by promoting MAVS degradation through distinct degradation pathways. In vivo, TRAF6 deficiency enhanced antiviral gene expression, reduced infectious viral titers, and significantly improved survival following SVCV infection. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized dual regulatory role for TRAF6 in fish antiviral immunity and highlight the importance of TRAF6-mediated MAVS degradation under basal conditions in regulating IFN-mediated antiviral responses.

Journal of Virology.title: Non-classical human astrovirus VA1 induces cell line-specific increases in intestinal epithelial permeability associated with claudin remodeling.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Astroviruses are non-enveloped viruses with a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome. Human astroviruses (HAstVs) are classified into classical strains (HAstV-1 to HAstV-8) and non-classical strains (VA1-6 and MLB1-3). These viruses typically cause self-resolving acute gastroenteritis, but symptoms can be more severe, including extraintestinal infections and viral encephalitis, especially in vulnerable groups, such as children and the immunocompromised. Despite being one of the leading causes of pediatric gastroenteritis worldwide, little is known about the pathogenic mechanisms, and no vaccines or antivirals currently exist. Tight junctions are formed by multiprotein complexes, including claudins and occludin, that separate the intestinal lumen from the host interior and play an important role in intestinal barrier maintenance. HAstV-1 disrupts these tight junctions in polarized Caco-2 monolayers by degrading occludin and E-cadherin, thereby decreasing intestinal barrier permeability. In contrast, this study demonstrated that VA1 decreases transepithelial electrical resistance in polarized T84, but not Caco-2, cells by altering protein levels and localization of select claudins. Specifically, western blot analysis of T84, but not Caco-2, protein lysates showed that protein expression of the pore-forming claudin-2 increased in infected cells, while protein levels of sealing claudins-4 and -18 decreased. In addition, immunofluorescence imaging indicated a relocalization of claudin-3 into the cytosol. Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid bacterial metabolite found in the intestine, attenuated these barrier changes. These data demonstrate that VA1 induces cell type-specific claudin remodeling associated with decreased epithelial barrier permeability in T84 cells and highlight the differences between classical and non-classical HAstVs in the mechanisms underlying intestinal barrier remodeling.IMPORTANCEHuman astroviruses are prevalent enteric viruses that are a leading cause of pediatric gastroenteritis worldwide. However, little is known about their pathogenic mechanisms, and no vaccines or antivirals are available to treat or prevent infections. Herein, we demonstrate that VA1 infection induces changes in the electrical conductance of polarized T84 cell monolayers and alters claudin protein levels or their cellular localization. This phenotype is attenuated by pre-treatment with the bacterial short-chain fatty acid butyrate and is not observed in infected polarized Caco-2 monolayers. Collectively, these data suggest that VA1 induces cell type-specific barrier alterations through claudin remodeling that differ from the HAstV-1-induced alterations in tight junction complex proteins occludin and E-cadherin, highlighting virus-specific differences in pathogenic mechanisms of classical and non-classical HAstVs.

Journal of Virology.title: A human sensory neuron model for varicella-zoster virus latency and reactivation in vitro.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is a ubiquitous human neurotropic alphaherpesvirus that establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglionic neurons. Subsequent viral reactivation causes herpes zoster, a morbid disease often complicated by neuropathic pain. Mechanisms underlying VZV latency and reactivation are not understood, mostly due to the lack of permissive animal models and challenges of current in vitro latency modeling. Here, we evaluated HD10.6 cells, a simplified and easily expandable human sensory neuron line to model VZV latency and reactivation. Differentiated HD10.6 (dHD10.6) neurons supported productive VZV infection, viral DNA replication, production of infectious progeny, and viral spread in cultures. VZV infection was associated with limited cytopathic effects and ultrastructural changes. Infecting dHD10.6 neurons with cell-free VZV in the presence of antivirals resulted in a quiescent-persistent state, characterized by persistent VZV genomes with restricted VZV gene expression and absence of infectious virus. Importantly, VZV could be reactivated by treatment with capsaicin, as evidenced by increased lytic viral transcription and virus spread. In conclusion, this study establishes human HD10.6 neurons as a novel and expandable in vitro model for studying VZV latency and reactivation to identify virus and host factors governing latency that may serve as therapeutic targets to restrict VZV reactivation.IMPORTANCEMost individuals carry latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in their dorsal root ganglia (DRG), which can reactivate to cause shingles and chronic pain. The mechanisms by which VZV establishes latency and triggers of reactivation are incompletely understood. Current platforms for the study of VZV latency do not easily support functional experiments (ganglia) or are difficult to expand and complicated by mixed neuronal populations (stem cell-derived neurons). Here, we demonstrate that differentiated HD10.6 cells derived from immortalized human DRG-derived neurons provide a clonal and easy-to-expand platform for studying lytic, latent, and reactivated VZV infection in sensory neurons. We propose that the HD10.6 platform could provide the basis to conduct studies on the viral latent state that have hitherto not been possible.

Journal of Virology.title: Salty virus-host interactions: infection mechanisms of haloarchaeal viruses HRTV-7 and HRTV-10.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Archaea can be infected by morphologically diverse viruses, and the study of these viruses is important for understanding viral evolution in general. Archaeal tailed viruses make up the largest group of isolated archaeal viruses and the major class of isolated viruses infecting haloarchaea. Yet, little is known about the infection strategies of these viruses. In this study, we focus on archaeal myoviruses and investigate their infection cycles. HRTV-7 and HRTV-10 are both capable of infecting multiple Halorubrum strains, including Halorubrum salinarum B2-2, which is well suited for light microscopy. Virus lifecycle experiments combined with plaque assays and time-lapse microscopy showed that both viruses have a predominantly lytic life cycle, with complete lysis occurring between 9 and 12 h post-infection. Cells swell considerably just prior to lysis, indicating that the cell envelope becomes compromised. Whole-genome sequencing of virus-insensitive strains suggests that HRTV-10 likely uses the S-layer, the main cell envelope component of these archaea, as a receptor. Interestingly, we observed full-length integration of HRTV-7 in virus-resistant cells, as well as parts of the viral genome within the host genome, suggesting viral resistance based on superinfection exclusion. Together, these findings contribute to our understanding of archaeal virus-host interactions and provide insight into their infection strategies.IMPORTANCEViruses of archaea are important to understand the diversity and evolution of all viruses. However, they are little studied. Archaea are ubiquitous microorganisms, of which some thrive at extreme conditions, such as high salt concentrations. Salt-loving haloarchaea are excellent models to study archaeal virus-host interactions due to the high availability of viral isolates and suitability for microscopy. Bacteria and archaea are both infected by tailed viruses; however, in archaea, their infection mechanisms are largely unknown. We used two tailed archaeal viruses infecting the same host to compare their infection strategies. Both viruses induce cell lysis of the host, which is preceded by cell bloating. Interestingly, one of the viruses can integrate into the genome of the host, which renders the strain resistant, suggesting a mechanism of superinfection exclusion. This work provides insight into archaeal virus-host interactions, thereby contributing to the exploration of the unusual archaeal virosphere.

mBio.title: Ehrlichia chaffeensis and its retropepsin-type protease engage the complement inhibitor C4b-binding protein.
mBio.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Ehrlichia chaffeensis is a tick-borne obligate intracellular bacterium that causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis. Significant advances have been made in understanding immune evasion strategies in Ehrlichia; however, the role of the complement system has been largely overlooked. This study provides evidence for a novel interaction between E. chaffeensis and the complement inhibitor C4b-binding protein (C4BP). We confirmed that E. chaffeensis recruits and binds C4BP at its surface, demonstrating binding of C4BP in human serum. This interaction is concentration-dependent, and C4BP retains its regulatory cofactor activity when bound to the bacteria. Furthermore, we identified the ehrlichial retropepsin-type protease-named APEhc-as a new C4BP ligand. We show that the soluble domain of APEhc targets multiple serum components, directly binding factor H, forming complexes with C4BP, and cleaving two major complement components, C3b and C4b. Quantitative binding analysis reveals a strong interaction between APEhc and C4BP, with apparent dissociation constants in the nanomolar range. Analysis of C4BP CCP deletion mutants supports a contribution of CCP3, CCP6, and CCP7 to APEhc-C4BP binding. Additionally, we demonstrate that C4BP retains its factor I cofactor activity in the presence of APEhc, and that APEhc independently cleaves C4b. Consistent with the targeting and modulation of serum components, our results show that APEhc significantly inhibits activation of the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways. Our findings reveal the unprecedented interaction between E. chaffeensis, its retropepsin protease, and complement inhibitors, raising intriguing questions regarding complement targeting by E. chaffeensis and its role in immune evasion. [IMPORTANCE] Human monocytic ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne disease caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, which can be severe or fatal if untreated. Understanding how E. chaffeensis evades the immune system is crucial for identifying new virulence factors and developing new treatments. The complement system, an essential part of the body's first line of defense, is often targeted by pathogens to avoid immune attacks. We show that E. chaffeensis binds to C4b-binding protein (C4BP), a major inhibitor of the classical pathway (CP) and lectin pathway (LP), and identify the ehrlichial retropepsin-type protease, APEhc, as a novel C4BP ligand. Additionally, we demonstrate that APEhc targets other serum components, inhibiting complement CP, LP, and AP activation, suggesting an unprecedented dual-inhibitory activity for APEhc through complex formation with C4BP (and factor H) and cleavage of C3b and C4b. Our findings reveal a multifunctional role for APEhc in immune evasion, raising intriguing questions about the mechanisms used by intracellular pathogens like E. chaffeensis to bypass host defenses.

mBio.title: Targeting sterylglucosidase 1 attenuates virulence and enables immune protection against Candida albicans.
mBio.abstract: Sterylglucosidases are fungus-specific enzymes that regulate ergosterol 3-β-D-glucoside (Erg-SG) homeostasis and represent promising targets for antifungal intervention. Previous studies demonstrated that sterylglucosidases from Cryptococcus neoformans and Aspergillus fumigatus contribute to fungal virulence, and that deletion of these enzymes elicits protective immunity. However, whether sterylglucosidase-mediated pathways similarly influence Candida albicans pathogenicity remains unknown. Here, we identified C. albicans Sgl1 as a bona fide sterylglucosidase that selectively hydrolyzes Erg-SG but not fungal glucosylceramide. Deletion of SGL1 resulted in marked Erg-SG accumulation without altering glucosylceramide levels, confirming its conserved role in sterylglucoside homeostasis. Although the Δsgl1 mutant displayed largely preserved growth, morphogenesis, and stress adaptation, it exhibited impaired biofilm formation. Biochemical characterization, inhibitor profiling, and structural analyses revealed marked species-specific inhibitor susceptibility among fungal sterylglucosidases despite highly conserved overall architecture and catalytic machinery. Structural modeling and docking studies identified differences in ligand positioning and active-site interactions that likely contribute to these divergent pharmacological responses. Functionally, loss of SGL1 significantly attenuated virulence in a murine model of systemic candidiasis. Importantly, vaccination with heat-killed Δsgl1 cells conferred 70% protection against lethal systemic challenge and markedly reduced kidney fungal burden, providing the first evidence that sterylglucosidase-dependent vaccination can induce protective immunity against a non-pulmonary fungal infection. Collectively, these findings establish C. albicans Sgl1 as a conserved regulator of sterylglucoside homeostasis, fungal pathogenicity, and host protection, and identify fungal sterylglucosidases as promising targets for antifungal drug and immunotherapy development.IMPORTANCEFungal infections are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, yet effective immunotherapies and novel antifungal targets remain limited. Candida albicans is a major cause of invasive and mucosal fungal disease, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. Here, we identify the fungus-specific sterylglucosidase Sgl1 as a conserved regulator of ergosterol 3-β-D-glucoside homeostasis and a critical determinant of C. albicans pathogenicity. We further demonstrate that fungal sterylglucosidases exhibit distinct species-specific pharmacological responses despite conserved structural frameworks, revealing opportunities for rational antifungal drug design. Importantly, deletion of SGL1 attenuated virulence and enabled protective vaccination against lethal systemic candidiasis, providing the first evidence that targeting sterylglucoside metabolism can elicit protective immunity against a non-pulmonary fungal pathogen. Together, these findings identify Candida albicans Sgl1 as a promising target for antifungal drug and immunotherapy development.

mBio.title: Broad use of feline APN by alphacoronaviruses implicates cats in cross-species transmission.
mBio.abstract: Coronaviruses continue to pose a global public health threat, and the increasing frequency of zoonotic spillover events highlights the crucial role of animal hosts in cross-species transmission. As companion animals, cats warrant attention for their potential involvement in coronavirus cross-species spread. Here, we show that feline aminopeptidase N (fAPN) functions as a shared receptor utilized by multiple alphacoronaviruses (α-CoVs), including human coronavirus 229E (HCoV-229E), transmissible gastroenteritis virus, and type-II feline infectious peritonitis virus, to mediate entry into feline cells. Structural and functional analyses reveal that distinct viruses engage fAPN through alternative binding sites, enabling multimodal receptor recognition, and demonstrating notable receptor compatibility. Animal challenge experiments further indicate that HCoV-229E showed detectable viral RNA and infectious virus in the feline respiratory tract, with no apparent clinical signs. Together, these findings establish fAPN as a shared receptor for diverse α-CoVs and reveal a molecular basis for receptor compatibility across viral lineages, providing insight into the determinants of coronavirus host range and cross-species transmission.IMPORTANCEZoonotic coronaviruses repeatedly threaten human health, yet the rules governing their ability to cross species remain incompletely understood. Cats live in close contact with humans and may act as hidden hosts for coronaviruses, but the molecular basis supporting cross-species infection in these animals is unclear. This study demonstrates that feline aminopeptidase N (fAPN) serves as a common receptor for several alphacoronaviruses (α-CoVs), including human coronavirus 229E (HCoV-229E), transmissible gastroenteritis virus, and type-II feline infectious peritonitis virus. These viruses recognize fAPN through distinct binding sites, highlighting the flexibility of receptor recognition. Additionally, HCoV-229E inoculation resulted in detectable viral RNA in the respiratory tract of cats, without apparent clinical signs. These results help explain why α-CoVs can move across host barriers and suggest that cats should be considered when assessing coronavirus spillover risks at the human-animal interface.

mBio.title: Decoding the cefazolin inoculum effect: phenotypic and genotypic insights beyond the MIC.
mBio.abstract: The cefazolin inoculum effect (CzIE) is a clinically relevant in vitro phenomenon that may compromise cefazolin efficacy in high-inoculum methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections such as bacteremia and infective endocarditis. We aimed to define mechanisms underlying CzIE beyond BlaZ-dependent enzymatic pathways. We evaluated CzIE in 198 MSSA isolates (single center) by comparing minimum inhibitory concentrations at standard and high inoculum. The inoculum effect index was used as a quantitative measure of the CzIE to validate the operational definition and assess its concordance with the classical definition of CzIE. Whole-genome sequencing was used to define β-lactamase gene (blaZ) allotypes, accessory gene regulator (agr) genotypes (I-IV), and clonal lineages. CzIE was observed in 16.16% of isolates, with Type A (71.9%) and Type C (28.1%) blaZ allotypes predominating among CzIE-positive strains. These isolates were enriched within clonal complex CC8 and CC30. Twenty-four-hour time-kill experiments combining cefazolin with BlaZ inhibitor (sulbactam) demonstrated initial killing followed by regrowth in CzIE-positive isolates, while complete eradication was observed in CzIE-negative isolates. Population analysis profiles (PAP) revealed the expansion of cefazolin-non-susceptible subpopulations at high inoculum, consistent with phenotypic heterogeneity. agr typing identified agrIII as the predominant genotype among CzIE-positive isolates, and agr dysfunction was significantly associated with CzIE-positive phenotype. Together, these findings suggest that CzIE is driven not only by BlaZ-mediated activity but also by agr-dependent regulatory pathways. These observations highlight the potential clinical importance of CzIE and support further investigation into its implications for therapeutic optimization and improved patient outcomes.IMPORTANCECefazolin inoculum effect (CzIE) represents an underrecognized potential determinant of therapeutic failure in methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections, yet it remains absent from routine susceptibility testing frameworks. We demonstrate that CzIE is not solely driven by blaZ-mediated activity but is strongly associated with agr-dependent regulation and population heterogeneity. Our findings suggest that standard MIC testing can underestimate cefazolin failure under high-inoculum conditions commonly encountered in invasive diseases. Importantly, identification of CzIE-positive isolates could inform therapeutic decision-making, including selection of alternative β-lactams or adjunctive strategies to suppress tolerant subpopulations. Integration of CzIE assessment with genomic markers such as blaZ allotype and agr genotype may enable more precise prediction of treatment response. These data provide a framework for incorporating CzIE into diagnostic workflows and guide future studies evaluating its clinical utility. Ultimately, recognizing CzIE as a multifactorial phenotype may improve antibiotic selection, reduce treatment failure, and enhance outcomes in serious MSSA infections across patient populations.

mBio.title: The BspC surface adhesin and gastrointestinal fungal colonization enhance group B streptococcal neonatal infection.
mBio.abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonizes the gastrointestinal (GI) and female reproductive tracts of up to 30% of healthy adults, but during pregnancy can be transmitted to the newborn, causing neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis. Neonatal GI colonization is an important precursor to invasive disease, yet the mechanisms governing GBS intestinal persistence and dissemination are still being elucidated. Given the predominance of hypervirulent sequence type 17 (ST-17) strains in neonatal invasive disease, we hypothesized that the ST-17-associated surface adhesin BspC contributes to gastrointestinal colonization and infection. Using a neonatal mouse model, we found that pups infected with wild-type GBS exhibited increased mortality and significantly higher bacterial burdens in the intestine, blood, spleen, and brain compared with pups infected with a ΔbspC mutant. We also observed that BspC promoted adherence to a 2D organoid model of the human infant colon and Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cells through its variable domain. Building on previous findings that Candida albicans interacts with BspC, we found that C. albicans enhanced GBS intestinal epithelial adherence in a BspC-dependent manner, and coinfection increased intestinal GBS burden and brain dissemination in neonatal mice. Finally, analysis of published human neonatal fecal microbiome data sets revealed higher GBS abundance in infants colonized with C. albicans or other Candida species. Together, these findings identify BspC as a key mediator of GBS intestinal colonization and invasive disease and suggest that fungal colonization of the neonatal GI promotes GBS pathogenesis.IMPORTANCEGroup B Streptococcus (GBS) is a leading cause of neonatal infection, which can result in fatality or long-term neurological morbidity in survivors. Intestinal colonization is an important precursor to invasive disease, yet the factors that promote GBS persistence in the neonatal gastrointestinal tract remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the GBS surface adhesin BspC as a mediator of intestinal epithelial adherence, gastrointestinal colonization, and systemic dissemination. We further demonstrate that the common fungal pathobiont Candida albicans enhances GBS intestinal adherence and infection. Consistent with our experimental findings, analysis of human infant microbiome data sets revealed greater GBS abundance in infants colonized with Candida species. These findings identify BspC as a key mediator of this process and suggest that fungal colonization can enhance GBS disease.

mBio.title: A σ(B)-dependent sRNA provides a repressor function to the general stress response in Clostridioides difficile.
mBio.abstract: Clostridioides difficile is an anaerobic, gram-positive gastrointestinal pathogen that poses a significant health threat worldwide. A recent RIL-seq characterization of the Hfq-mediated RNA-RNA interactome revealed that small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators of virulence-related processes in C. difficile, including the initiation of sporulation. In the model Proteobacteria species E. coli and S. enterica, sRNAs often function as non-coding elements in vital stress responses mediated by alternative sigma factors, acting as repressors within these regulatory networks. However, whether this principle is broadly conserved across bacterial phyla remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that the Hfq-dependent sRNA SrsA is part of the regulatory network of the alternative sigma factor σB, which governs the general stress response in Firmicutes. Consequently, SrsA is highly expressed during the transition from exponential to stationary phase and under infection-related stress conditions, such as oxidative stress. We show that SrsA represses a highly conserved small protein family that regulates sporulation and three genes in the methyl-fixing branch of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway (WLP). Infection of mice further revealed that SrsA contributes to disease severity and bacterial recovery from antibiotic treatment in an acute and relapse mouse model of C. difficile infection. In summary, our data suggest that integrating SrsA into the σB regulon helps coordinate sporulation and vital metabolic pathways of C. difficile in response to infection-relevant stress conditions.IMPORTANCEThe central role of sRNAs as non-coding arms of stress responses represents a paradigm of sRNA function in Gammaproteobacteria. However, it remains unclear how broadly this regulatory principle is conserved across the bacterial tree of life. In our study, we identified the sRNA SrsA as a non-coding regulator involved in the sigma B-mediated stress response to nutrient limitation and radical stress in the intestinal pathogen Clostridioides difficile. We demonstrate that SrsA suppresses the production of a conserved family of spore regulators and of enzymes of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, establishing a role in regulating sporulation and gut colonization. Our work provides novel insights into the regulation of the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, which is usually associated with autotrophic bacteria, and highlights the metabolic flexibility this anaerobic gut pathogen has evolved to survive in a nutrient-limited and inflamed gut environment.

mBio.title: RasGAP and Crk bind Anaplasma phagocytophilum effector AteA at tyrosine-phosphorylated EPLYA motifs.
mBio.abstract: Host cell signaling networks play critical roles in responding to bacterial infections. Intracellular pathogens manipulate these signals to establish a replicative niche in the host cell. Vector-borne rickettsial pathogens, such as Anaplasma phagocytophilum, encounter the dual challenge of interfacing with cell signaling in both the mammalian host and the tick vector Ixodes scapularis. A central feature that enables A. phagocytophilum survival in both mammals and ticks is the type 4 secretion system (T4SS), which secretes effector proteins into the host cell to manipulate biological processes. Only a few A. phagocytophilum T4SS effectors have been experimentally tested, primarily in mammalian cells. While AteA has been identified as the first T4SS effector known to be essential for A. phagocytophilum survival in the tick, its molecular targets in the tick remained unknown. Here, we investigated AteA interactions with tick cell proteins and a possible mechanism of AteA activation. AteA contains multiple EPIYA-like short linear motifs with the consensus sequence EPLYA. Other known bacterial EPIYA motif effectors, including AnkA from A. phagocytophilum, target mammalian phosphotyrosine signaling proteins. We found that AteA is tyrosine-phosphorylated at EPLYA motifs by the non-receptor tyrosine kinases Src and Abl in eukaryotic cells and during tick infection. Protein pull-down assays revealed that Ixodes SH2 domain-containing proteins, RasGAP and Crk, preferentially interact with phosphorylated AteA EPLYA motifs. RasGAP and Crk have interconnected roles in cell signaling, suggesting that A. phagocytophilum targets these pathways during infection of the arthropod vector.IMPORTANCETick-borne diseases are on the rise globally, linked to changes in climate, land use, and human-animal interactions. Interrupting vector-borne transmission requires understanding how the vector and pathogens interact. Recent studies have shown ticks detect and respond to pathogens through cellular immune and stress signaling pathways. We previously demonstrated that the tick-borne bacterium Anaplasma phagocytophilum encodes a tick-specific secreted effector, AteA, that is essential for the pathogen's survival in the tick. Here, we showed that AteA is phosphorylated by tick cell kinases, which promotes binding to host cell SH2 domain-containing proteins that are integral to cellular signaling networks. Understanding how these interactions affect signaling pathways in the tick will be essential if interventions targeting the vector are to be developed.

mBio.title: The cell wall integrity pathway kinase Mpk1 regulates extracellular vesicle production and apoptotic-like vesicle release in Cryptococcus neoformans.
mBio.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are important mediators of fungal physiology and host interactions, yet the mechanisms governing their production remain poorly understood. In Cryptococcus neoformans, EV production is tightly regulated by environmental conditions, suggesting the existence of dedicated signaling pathways. Here, we screened a kinase deletion library to identify regulators of EV production and found that the cell wall integrity (CWI) pathway acts as a major negative regulator of EV production. Deletion of the CWI kinases MPK1, MKK2, or BCK1 increased EV release. Unexpectedly, the size of EVs produced by CWI mutants differed markedly from wild type. Accordingly, cryo-electron microscopy revealed the accumulation of larger vesicles with altered size distributions in the mpk1Δ mutant. These EVs lacked the characteristic mannoprotein-based fibrillar surface decoration observed on most wild-type vesicles, exhibited reduced association with capsular polysaccharide, and contained substantially less protein. Quantitative proteomic analysis demonstrated extensive remodeling of the EV proteome, with depletion of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins, and enrichment of ribosomal proteins and histones. Finally, mpk1Δ EVs displayed several hallmarks of mammalian apoptotic EVs, including phosphatidylserine exposure, and were produced under conditions associated with reduced cell viability. Together, these findings identify the CWI pathway as a central regulator of fungal EV production and provide evidence that C. neoformans produces distinct EV populations through genetically regulated pathways. Our results provide evidence for an apoptotic-like EV population in fungi and reveal an unexpected link between cell wall integrity signaling, cell death, and EV diversity.IMPORTANCEFungal extracellular vesicles (EVs) contribute to virulence, antifungal resistance, and host-pathogen interactions, yet the mechanisms governing their production remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the cell wall integrity signaling pathway as a major regulator of EV production in the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. We further show that disruption of one of the major kinases of this pathway induces the production of a distinct population of EVs with structural and molecular features resembling mammalian apoptotic EVs. These findings demonstrate that fungi produce multiple EV populations through genetically regulated pathways rather than a single constitutive mechanism. By establishing the existence of apoptotic-like EVs in fungi, our work provides new insight into fungal EV production and lays the foundation for investigating how different EV populations contribute to fungal physiology, pathogenesis, and antifungal resistance.

mBio.title: Theft of host transferrin receptor-1 by Toxoplasma gondii is required for infection.
mBio.abstract: Host nutrient acquisition is essential for apicomplexan parasite infection, yet mechanisms underpinning this are not defined. We discovered the genome of Toxoplasma gondii lacks conserved genes for iron transport and storage and these host cell proteins, including the transferrin receptor 1, transferrin, ferritin heart/heavy and liver/light chains, and clathrin light chain, are robustly taken up by tachyzoites. Acquisition of these host cell proteins was conserved across host cell species and parasite virulence types. Increased trafficking of host cell transferrin receptor 1 to endolysosomes boosted tachyzoite acquisition of host proteins and growth rate. Bradyzoites possessed little capacity to acquire host cell proteins, consistent with the cyst wall representing a barrier to host cell protein cargo. This study provides insight into essential functions associated with parasite theft of host iron acquisition and storage proteins.IMPORTANCEHost nutrient theft is a dogmatic principle of parasitism. The paradigm that Toxoplasma gondii avoids association with host proteins, seemingly abstaining from them as a nutritional stream and for immune system avoidance, is changing. Many host proteins are enriched at the parasitophorous vacuole, but that barrier may be breached since exogenous proteins expressed by host cells transverse to T. gondii bodies. Our work presented here provides in vivo context to this new view because several host iron homeostatic proteins are acquired and retained within the parasite to support infection. These findings not only shed light on how T. gondii could acquire iron but also reveal new host-parasite interactions of theft and integration of host proteins by pathogens.

mBio.title: The core interaction network of transcription elongation factors is broadly maintained across diverse bacteria.
mBio.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Bacterial transcription elongation has been investigated most thoroughly for the model bacterium Escherichia coli. The E. coli elongation factor NusG associates through its N-terminal domain with the transcription elongation complex (TEC), while its C-terminal domain forms mutually exclusive interactions with either ribosomal protein S10 or Rho termination factor. The E. coli NusG:S10 complex bridges the TEC with a pioneering ribosome for coupling of transcription and translation. NusG also participates in antitermination complexes (ATC) that inhibit Rho-dependent termination and increase transcription of rRNA operons. A characteristic sequence in the nascent rrn RNA, called boxA, loads E. coli NusB:S10 onto the NusG-bound TEC, leading to the formation of the rrn ATC. However, these findings may not extend to all bacteria. Rho-dependent termination is less important in gram-positive bacteria, including some that do not encode Rho, and transcription and translation remain uncoupled in Bacillus subtilis and many other gram-positive bacteria. It is therefore unclear whether the interaction network for E. coli elongation factors is conserved in these organisms. We identified boxA-like sequences upstream of 16S and 23S genes in Bacillus species and found that they associate directly with NusB. We also found that B. subtilis S10 associates with both NusB and NusG, and that Rho can also associate with NusG. Bioinformatic analyses revealed conservation of interaction interface residues across multiple phyla. Together, these data demonstrate that the core interaction network of bacterial elongation factors is broadly conserved across diverse bacteria, despite differences in how these interactions function in individual species. [IMPORTANCE] Escherichia coli is known to use several key elongation factors that promote direct coupling of transcription with translation. These factors also trigger the formation of an antitermination complex that protects the synthesis of ribosomal RNA and CRISPR transcripts from interference by the Rho termination factor. However, Bacillus subtilis is not thought to couple transcription with translation. It is also not known whether B. subtilis needs to suppress Rho, given that its Rho is dispensable. Therefore, we purified B. subtilis elongation factors and mapped their interaction network. Surprisingly, we find that the B. subtilis elongation factors form complexes that closely resemble E. coli counterparts, despite the significant mechanistic differences in how these bacteria control transcription elongation.

mBio.title: mGem: Antibiotic tolerance across the growth-rate continuum in chronic human infections.
mBio.abstract: Antibiotic failure is frequently attributed to genetic resistance, yet many chronic infections persist despite clinical isolates remaining susceptible to antibiotics. Antibiotic tolerance offers an alternative explanation, but is commonly interpreted through persisters, dormancy, and growth arrest. We argue this theory is incomplete. In vitro studies consistently demonstrate that growth rate strongly influences antibiotic susceptibility, while bacteria in chronic human infections occupy a broad continuum of growth states. However, experimental models of tolerance largely examine rapidly growing or growth-arrested bacteria and rarely encompass the substantially slower growth rates found in chronic infection. We propose that tolerance can emerge from stochastic growth-rate heterogeneity within clonal populations without requiring transition into dormancy. Thus, understanding tolerance requires defining how antibiotic survival changes across the growth-rate continuum. Further studies directly examining antibiotic tolerance at slow growth rates representative of chronic infection are needed to understand tolerance during human infection.

mBio.title: TriLock-FISH enables in situ discrimination of influenza cRNA and mRNA for single-cell analysis of viral replication and transcription.
mBio.abstract: Influenza A virus produces three RNA species-viral RNA (vRNA), complementary RNA (cRNA), and messenger RNA (mRNA)-whose synthesis and trafficking are spatially compartmentalized. However, the high sequence similarity between cRNA and mRNA hinders their distinction in situ, limiting understanding of the spatial organization of the viral replication-transcription dynamics. Here, triple-lock fluorescence in situ hybridization (TriLock-FISH) was developed to distinguish vRNA, cRNA, and mRNA in situ with high specificity. TriLock-FISH enabled a genome-wide, time-resolved single-cell atlas of RNA abundance and localization, revealing marked cell-to-cell variation in RNA abundance but relatively conserved spatial organization. cRNA was found to be predominantly nuclear, with a small but reproducible cytoplasmic fraction. Application to infected mouse lung tissue demonstrated simultaneous spatial detection of all viral RNA species. This approach provides a highly specific framework for single-cell analysis of RNA virus replication and transcription.IMPORTANCEInfluenza virus relies on three closely related RNA molecules for replication and gene expression, yet distinguishing them inside infected cells has remained technically challenging. This limitation has hindered understanding of viral replication in space and time. We developed triple-lock fluorescence in situ hybridization, which enables simultaneous visualization of all three viral RNA species across all eight influenza genome segments in infected cells and tissues. Single-cell analysis revealed striking heterogeneity in viral RNA abundance across infected cells, whereas intracellular RNA localization patterns remained relatively conserved. Complementary RNA, a replication intermediate long thought to be strictly nuclear, was also detected at low levels in the cytoplasm. These findings provide new insight into influenza virus replication and establish a broadly applicable tool for studying RNA virus biology.

mBio.title: The lumpy skin disease virus protein LSDV003 regulates MHC-I trafficking and surface expression.
mBio.abstract: Lumpy skin disease (LSD) is a severe transboundary disease of cattle caused by lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV), which is highly transmissible and responsible for substantial economic losses worldwide. Although cellular immune responses are critical for controlling poxvirus infections, the viral strategies used by LSDV to evade cytotoxic T-cell immunity remain poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that LSDV infection markedly downregulates major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) surface expression in host cells. Screening of LSDV-encoded proteins identified LSDV003 as a key viral factor responsible for MHC-I downregulation. Mechanistically, LSDV003 interacts with both the MHC-I heavy chain and β2-microglobulin and mediates endoplasmic reticulum (ER) retention of MHC-I via a C-terminal HNEL motif, thereby preventing its transport to the cell surface. Mutational analyses demonstrated that disruption of the HNEL motif impaired the ability of LSDV003 to alter MHC-I localization and surface expression. Furthermore, an LSDV003-deficient virus exhibited a markedly reduced capacity to suppress MHC-I surface expression. Collectively, these findings identify LSDV003 as a viral regulator of MHC-I trafficking and reveal a mechanism by which LSDV modulates host immune recognition.IMPORTANCELumpy skin disease is a highly contagious viral disease of cattle that has spread rapidly across Afro-Eurasia and causes major economic losses. However, the mechanisms used by lumpy skin disease virus to evade host immune defenses remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identify a previously unrecognized lumpy skin disease virus protein, LSDV003, that reduces the surface expression of major histocompatibility complex class I molecules in infected cells. We found that LSDV003 prevents these molecules from leaving the endoplasmic reticulum by using a C-terminal retention motif, thereby altering their normal intracellular trafficking. An LSDV003-deficient virus showed a reduced ability to suppress major histocompatibility complex class I surface expression during infection. These findings reveal an important immune evasion strategy used by lumpy skin disease virus and highlight LSDV003 as a potential target for improved vaccines and antiviral approaches to control this economically important disease.

mBio.title: Atypical E3 ligase HOIL1 promotes MDA5 signaling and ester-linked ubiquitination of LGP2.
mBio.abstract: The RIG-I-like receptors, RIG-I and MDA5, are innate sensors of RNA virus infections that are critical for mounting a robust antiviral immune response. Heme-oxidized IRP2 ligase 1 (HOIL1), a component of the linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex (LUBAC), is essential for interferon induction in response to viruses sensed by MDA5, but not viruses sensed by RIG-I; however, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. LUBAC contains two atypical E3 ubiquitin ligases, HOIL1 and HOIP. While HOIP generates "linear" polyubiquitin chains, HOIL1 catalyzes ester-linked ubiquitination of serine and threonine residues and glucosaccharides. Here, we show that HOIL1 E3 ligase activity is critical for MDA5-dependent interferon induction, whereas HOIP E3 ligase activity plays a minor role. Mechanistically, HOIL1 E3 ligase activity was required for MDA5 translocation to mitochondrion-associated membranes and the formation of MAVS aggregates. We further identified LGP2, a positive regulator of MDA5 oligomerization, as a HOIL1-interacting protein and substrate for ester-linked ubiquitination. In mice, loss of HOIL1 or its E3 ligase activity markedly impaired early interferon responses following infection with viruses sensed by MDA5. While HOIL1 deficiency resulted in increased viral burden and reduced survival, loss of HOIL1 ligase activity alone did not, indicating that HOIL1 exerts additional functions during antiviral immunity. Collectively, these findings establish ester-linked ubiquitination by HOIL1 as a critical mechanism regulating MDA5 signaling.IMPORTANCEThe rapid and robust production of interferon is critical for controlling viral infections. Cytoplasmic RNA sensors, RIG-I and MDA5, detect infection with distinct groups of viruses, leading to the transcriptional induction of interferon. However, inappropriate production of interferon triggered by aberrant MDA5 activation by cellular RNAs causes severe inflammatory disorders. Here, we report that the ubiquitin ligase activity of heme-oxidized IRP2 ligase 1 (HOIL1) is critical for the production of interferon in response to viruses that are sensed by MDA5 in cells and mice.
