Here, we converted C. difficile from an organism that relies primarily on 3-3 crosslinks made by LDTs to one that relies exclusively on 4-3 crosslinks made by an alternative family of crosslinking enzymes, the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs). Our findings explain why 3-3 crosslinking predominates over 4-3 crosslinking, clarify why C. difficile does not compensate for the loss of LDTs by increasing PBP activity, and suggest a model for how PBPs and LDTs work together in this problematic pathogen.

mBio.title: Neutrophil degranulation and extracellular ROS production are inactivated by Yersinia pseudotuberculosis YopE through a SKAP2 independent pathway.
mBio.abstract: Upon sensing Yersinia pseudotuberculosis (Yptb), receptor-mediated pathways are stimulated to trigger polymorphonuclear (PMN) antimicrobial responses. Yptb injects multiple type 3 secreted effector proteins, Yops (Yersinia outer proteins), that possess distinct biochemical functions, into PMNs to inhibit PMN responses. We show that several Yops, YopE, YopH, and YopO, each partially interfered with CD63 plasma membrane localization, a marker for primary degranulation. The host pathways involved in CD63 mobilization are complex, and it is not completely understood how Yops collaborate to inactivate this process. Here, CRISPR/Cas9 technology was used in an immortalized system of myeloid progenitor cells (Cas9-ER-HoxB8) to generate knockout PMN cell lines. To probe the impact of different Yops on the neutrophil pathways activated upon encountering Yptb, we interrogated the panel of genetically modified neutrophils with genetically modified bacteria. This approach of targeted gene deletion to inactivate specific pathways/proteins uncovered host pathways that synergize to induce CD63 mobilization that are distinctly targeted by YopE and YopH. YopE inhibited CD63 mobilization in the absence of SKAP2, a YopH target, whereas YopH inhibited CD63 mobilization in the absence of RhoG, a YopE target, indicating that these Yops inactivate distinct signaling pathways. Furthermore, the SKAP2-independent pathway inactivated by YopE is involved in primary granule release and ROS production. Overall, this work highlights multiple signaling pathways involved in mounting degranulation and ROS production and the diverse Yop-mediated mechanisms that WT-Yptb employs to effectively disarm them. Importantly, this work provides an avenue to untangle neutrophil signaling pathways targeted by pathogens using Cas9-ER-HoxB8 cells.IMPORTANCEWhen sensing invading bacteria, neutrophils become activated through multiple receptors that trigger signal-transduction cascades resulting in the generation of antimicrobial responses. The enteric pathogen, Yersinia pseudotuberculosis (Yptb), is equipped to effectively inhibit these responses using its collection of effector proteins (Yops). Here, we developed a system to overcome the limitations of performing genetic manipulations in neutrophils by implementing CRISPR/Cas9 technology in an engineered system of myeloid progenitor cells (Cas9-ER-HoxB8), which can be induced to differentiate into neutrophils. By infecting genetically modified neutrophils with Yptb strains expressing individual Yops, we identified distinct host signaling pathways that synergize to induce neutrophil antimicrobial responses. Our findings provide insight into several signaling events triggered by Yptb infection and show how YopE and YopH target distinct pathways to block vesicle trafficking and extracellular ROS production. This powerful genetic system can be applied to other pathogens to dissect the intricacies of neutrophil-pathogen interactions.

mBio.title: Cellular organization and phylogeny of Cryptonaiada gen. n. (Cryptonaiadidae fam. n.) shed light on the evolution of intracellular vertebrate parasitism in Apicomplexa.
mBio.abstract: Apicomplexan parasites have coevolved with animal hosts for hundreds of millions of years, yet only a handful of their lineages have made the transition to infecting vertebrates. Among the least understood vertebrate-infecting apicomplexans is Nematopsis temporariae, recently rediscovered after nearly a century of neglect. Here, we isolated this parasite from tadpole tissues and examined its host relationship, ultrastructure, and phylogenetic placement. We show that N. temporariae's monozoic oocysts are persistently associated with hepatic Kupffer cells in tadpoles of several frog species and undergo maturation within them, while being absent from adult hosts. Sporozoites possess a folded multimembrane pellicle, numerous paraglycogen granules, and an apical complex with polar rings and rhoptries. Exceptionally abundant micronemes are distributed throughout the cell rather than restricted to the apical region. Although several traits superficially resemble Nematopsis eugregarines from marine bivalves, single- and multi-gene phylogenies demonstrate that N. temporariae belongs to a distinct, distantly related lineage of freshwater actinocephaloid eugregarines. This evidence warrants the establishment of the new genus Cryptonaiada gen. n. in the new family Cryptonaiadidae fam. n.-the first known gregarine apicomplexan to have evolved vertebrate parasitism. We propose that Cryptonaiada develops within macrophages upon engulfment, evading digestion, and actively modulating them through sporozoite-mediated secretion. The persistent intracellular interaction between Cryptonaiada and tadpole macrophages may represent an early stage in parasite coevolution with vertebrate adaptive immunity, coinciding with a window of host immunological immaturity. Our findings highlight the value of studying neglected symbionts of amphibians, a group facing a significant global population decline.IMPORTANCEHow parasites evolve to infect vertebrate hosts with adaptive immunity remains a major question in parasitology. Apicomplexans provide a unique perspective on this transition, as vertebrate parasitism has arisen in only a handful of ancient lineages. Here, we characterize Cryptonaiada temporaria, an early-branching freshwater apicomplexan infecting tadpoles. The evidence indicates that Cryptonaiada represents a new gregarine genus and family that have evolved to infect tadpoles intracellularly, via oocysts engulfed by and developing within liver macrophages. The ultrastructure of the oocyst containing a single sporozoite reveals a semi-open state combining features consistent with environmental defense and secretion into the host cell. Cryptonaiada is absent from metamorphosed adults, suggesting that it exploits a developmental window of reduced host immune competence. These findings reveal an unusual form of intracellular vertebrate parasitism in gregarines, providing new insight into the evolutionary transition of apicomplexans from invertebrate to vertebrate hosts.

mBio.title: Role of O-specific antigen expression in Pseudomonas aeruginosa pathogenicity.
mBio.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a versatile, opportunistic pathogen, well-known for its adaptability to the challenging conditions encountered during infection of the human host. In chronic biofilm-associated infections, variations in motility and LPS structure are commonly observed adaptive traits. In this study, we identified differences in the expression of the O-specific antigen (OSA) biosynthetic cluster as a key driver of motility variation among a large number of clinical PA14 clade isolates. Despite retaining flagellar presence and function, OSA-deficient mutants exhibited increased hydrophobicity, which enhanced surface attachment and, in turn, reduced surface motility while promoting biofilm formation. The modified lipopolysaccharide structure with a lack of OSA also resulted in increased serum sensitivity, reduced phagocytic uptake, increased aminoglycoside resistance, and enhanced expression of the type III secretion system. These findings suggest that the commonly observed loss of OSA in P. aeruginosa isolates recovered from chronically infected cystic fibrosis lungs may be selectively advantageous. Importantly, we demonstrate that clinically relevant phenotypes influenced by the presence of OSA, such as motility and antibiotic resistance, become detectable only under test conditions that promote bacterial attachment. Similarly, the role of OSA expression in bacterial pathogenicity is conditional, with neither its presence nor its absence uniformly favoring infection. Together, our findings support a model in which OSA expression may be beneficial during early infection, whereas reduced OSA expression may promote traits associated with persistence at later stages.IMPORTANCELoss of the O-specific antigens (OSA) in Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates recovered from chronically infected cystic fibrosis lungs is a commonly observed phenotype that may confer a selective advantage to this opportunistic pathogen. In this study, we demonstrate that P. aeruginosa strains lacking OSA become more adhesive, limiting their motility but enhancing biofilm formation. Furthermore, OSA-deficient strains exhibit increased serum sensitivity, while they are phagocytosed less, express elevated type III secretion system genes, and show enhanced antibiotic resistance. Our findings suggest that altered OSA expression may contribute to stage-dependent infection phenotypes, where reduced OSA expression during later stages drives biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance, thereby enabling persistence.

mBio.title: Metabolomics in microbiology: interrogating microbial physiology and interactions.
mBio.abstract: Metabolomics provides a direct window into microbial function by capturing the small molecules that reflect cellular activity and microbial interactions. Here, we highlight its diverse applications for microbiologists across both in vitro and in vivo models under dynamic biological and nutritional conditions, including variations in community complexity, medium composition, and exposure to exogenous compounds such as antibiotics. Through representative case studies, we demonstrate how metabolomics provides critical insights into microbial physiology and inter-organismal interactions. We also showcase examples of multiomics integration, in which metabolomics is combined with complementary approaches to enhance data interpretation and strengthen biological conclusions. Finally, we discuss key challenges in metabolomics data analysis and highlight emerging strategies to overcome these limitations.

mBio.title: A small molecule increases mycobacterial translation fidelity without a fitness cost by targeting ribosomal protein S5.
mBio.abstract: A central dogma of molecular biology is the "speed-accuracy trade-off," where ribosomes must slow down to ensure accurate protein synthesis. In mycobacteria, a high basal level of mistranslation at glutamine and asparagine codons, caused by an indirect tRNA aminoacylation pathway, promotes tolerance to the antibiotic rifampicin. While pharmacologically increasing translational fidelity is a promising strategy to combat antibiotic tolerance, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we screened 9,000 synthetic compounds and identified benzo[d]isoxazole-4,7-diones as a novel chemical class that reduces mycobacterial mistranslation. Medicinal chemistry optimization yielded a lead compound, 9787, with superior potency in decreasing mistranslation and reversing rifampicin tolerance. Using competitive chemical proteomics, we identified the 30S ribosomal protein S5 (RpS5) as the specific cellular target. Remarkably, compound 9787 enhances translational fidelity at concentrations that do not measurably impact the overall rate of protein synthesis. Our findings challenge the universality of the speed-accuracy trade-off, demonstrating that fidelity can be improved independently of translation speed. This work reveals that the ribosomal small subunit is a druggable target for modulating translational quality control, and introduces a new strategy for combating antibiotic-tolerant bacteria without the associated fitness cost of slowed translation.IMPORTANCEA fundamental principle in molecular biology holds that ribosomes face a trade-off between translation speed and accuracy: going faster means making more errors, while maintaining high fidelity requires slowing down. This study challenges that paradigm by identifying a small molecule that increases translational accuracy in mycobacteria without affecting the rate of protein synthesis. The compound targets ribosomal protein S5 and specifically reduces errors arising from physiologically mischarged tRNAs-a quality control problem distinct from the well-studied codon-anticodon mismatches. This form of mistranslation contributes to antibiotic tolerance in tuberculosis, making it a potential therapeutic target. Our findings reveal unexpected flexibility in how ribosomes maintain translation quality and suggest that pharmacologically increasing fidelity without the fitness cost of slowed protein synthesis may be an attractive strategy for combating antibiotic-tolerant bacteria.

mBio.title: MAVS maintains mitochondrial import competence and also limits RNA virus replication independently of interferon signaling.
mBio.abstract: Intrinsic, cell-autonomous antiviral defenses can restrict infection without involving paracrine interferon (IFN) programs. Previous studies have demonstrated the importance of intact mitochondrial homeostasis in antiviral immunity. Mitochondrial antiviral signaling (MAVS) protein is a critical adaptor molecule in the RLR pathway that regulates IFN production in response to RNA viral infections. Here, we identify a potent intrinsic antiviral immunity that is orchestrated through stable mitochondria. We further identify MAVS as a regulator of mitochondrial import machinery whose activity is required for an IFN-independent antiviral state. Loss of MAVS leads to severe mitochondrial fragmentation, depolarization, and mitophagy, accompanied by diminished mitochondrial bioenergetics and protein import. Mechanistically, MAVS maintains mitochondrial integrity by maintaining the expression and assembly of the translocase of the outer membrane complex and sustaining the abundance of its core components. Restoration of MAVS expression reverses these defects and reinstates a robust antiviral state. Remarkably, this mitochondrial-driven immunity efficiently restricts SARS-CoV-2 replication even under IFN-deficient conditions and operates alongside the IFN pathways during infection by RNA viruses, such as the Japanese encephalitis virus. Our findings reveal a mitochondrial maintenance function of MAVS that operates in parallel to, and independently of, canonical interferon signaling during RNA virus infection. These findings highlight mitochondrial integrity as a common determinant behind a broad, collective antiviral immunity that involves both intrinsic and IFN-dependent mechanisms.IMPORTANCEHow do mitochondria contribute to the intrinsic cellular antiviral defense even when the primary immune arsenal is silenced? This work reveals that MAVS, long known for triggering interferon, acts as a vital bridge that stabilizes mitochondria to impart a potent intrinsic antiviral state against RNA viruses. We show that MAVS serves as a structural guardian of the organelle, a function it orchestrates by stabilizing the translocase of the outer membrane complex, the essential gateway for mitochondrial protein import. When MAVS is lost or targeted by viruses like SARS-CoV-2 and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), this gateway collapses, leading to organelle failure that viruses exploit. Crucially, we demonstrate that MAVS can restrict viral replication entirely independently of traditional interferon signaling. This discovery shifts our understanding of MAVS from a simple signal transducer to a multidimensional protector. By safeguarding the cell's "powerhouse," MAVS provides a fundamental layer of intrinsic immunity that remains active even when other immune responses are evaded.

mBio.title: Chicken DDX60 potentiates dsRNA analog-induced IFN-β signaling through synergistic interaction with MDA5.
mBio.abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) viruses cause devastating economic losses to the global poultry industry by triggering severe diseases in chickens; however, the anti-dsRNA innate immune mechanism in this species remains poorly defined. Critical limitations include the lack of the mammalian retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) receptor (a core dsRNA sensor) and the unelucidated role of DEAD/H-box helicase DDX60 (a key antiviral factor in mammals) in chicken antiviral immunity. To address these knowledge gaps, we investigated the function and mechanism of chicken DDX60 (chDDX60) in anti-dsRNA innate immunity using chicken embryo fibroblast cells (CEFs) and DF-1 cells as in vitro models, combined with gene overexpression/knockdown, luciferase reporter assays, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), immunofluorescence, molecular docking, and stimulation with the dsRNA analog polyinosinic-polycytidylic acid (poly I:C). Our results showed that chDDX60 is highly expressed in immune-relevant tissues (small intestine and spleen), induces IFN-β and downstream antiviral genes (ISG15, MX-1, PKR) via activating IRF7, interacts with chMDA5 to synergistically enhance IFN-β activation, acts upstream of chMDA5 to trigger the chMDA5-chMAVS-chSTING-chIRF7-IFN-β signaling axis, and is essential for establishing an antiviral state against dsRNA viruses under poly I:C stimulation. Taken together, our findings identify chDDX60 as a positive regulator of dsRNA analog-induced IFN-β signaling in chicken cells and provide new insight into the regulation of RIG-I-like receptors (RLR)-mediated innate immune signaling in RIG-I-deficient avian species. Further studies using infectious RNA virus models are needed to determine whether chDDX60 contributes to antiviral defense against dsRNA and/or ssRNA viruses.IMPORTANCEViral RNA sensing is essential for host defense, but chickens naturally lack retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I), a major RNA sensor in mammals. This study shows that chicken DDX60 helps activate IFN-β signaling in response to the synthetic double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) analog polyinosinic-polycytidylic acid (poly I:C) by working together with melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5). Mechanistically, chDDX60 functions upstream of chMDA5 and promotes activation of the chMDA5-chMAVS-chSTING-chIRF7-IFN-β signaling axis. These findings help explain how chicken cells regulate RNA-triggered innate immune signaling despite the absence of RIG-I and provide insight into avian-specific antiviral immune regulation. Because this study did not use infectious RNA viruses, future studies using dsRNA and ssRNA virus models will be needed to define the antiviral function and virus-type specificity of chDDX60.

mBio.title: Two closely related β-1,2-xylosyltransferases differentially impact cryptococcal glycan synthesis.
mBio.abstract: Cryptococcus neoformans is an opportunistic fungal pathogen that causes pulmonary infection in immunocompromised patients, which in severe cases leads to fatal meningoencephalitis. Cryptococcus exhibits unique glycobiology that plays important roles in pathogenesis. Unlike model yeast and other common fungal pathogens, Cryptococcus incorporates xylose, a five-carbon monosaccharide, into its glycans. One trimer motif, which consists of xylose in β-1,2 linkage to the reducing mannose of an α-1,3-mannose dimer, occurs in key cryptococcal glycoconjugates that include protein N- and O-linked glycans, glycosylinositol phosphorylceramides (GIPCs), and the capsule polysaccharides glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal). We previously identified cryptococcal β-1,2-xylosyltransferase 1 (Cxt1), which catalyzes the formation of this motif in GIPCs, GXM, and GXMGal. Here, we report the discovery of a second enzyme, cryptococcal β-1,2-xylosyltransferase 2 (Cxt2). Through characterization of cells that lack one or both corresponding genes (CXT1 and CXT2), we have dissected the biological roles of these enzymes, which are overlapping but not identical. Notably, Cxt1 and Cxt2 colocalize in the Golgi, influence the capsule in a strain-dependent manner, and together are responsible for all xylose addition to O-glycans. Overall, our work highlights the unique roles of these two enzymes and fills a gap in our understanding of cryptococcal glycan synthesis.IMPORTANCECryptococcus neoformans is an opportunistic fungal pathogen that causes almost 150,000 deaths each year worldwide. Cryptococcus synthesizes unique glycan structures that play important roles in its biology and pathogenesis. One abundant component of these structures is xylose, a five-carbon monosaccharide. Because xylose is not used by many fungal organisms, including model yeast, we have limited information about how cells add it to their glycans. Here we report a xylosyltransferase enzyme that performs this function, and we characterize specific biological roles of this protein and a closely related one we discovered earlier. We find that these proteins together perform all detectable xylose addition to an important class of protein-linked glycans (O-glycans). They also both participate in other synthetic processes, although this varies with the specific enzyme and strain background. These results contribute to our understanding of cryptococcal glycan synthesis and underscore the importance of testing multiple background strains.

mBio.title: A generalizable framework for genetic code expansion in bacterial systems beyond E. coli.
mBio.abstract: Genetic code expansion (GCE) enables the site-specific incorporation of noncanonical amino acids into proteins, providing a powerful platform to investigate and engineer biological functions with molecular precision. While GCE has facilitated transformative studies in Escherichia coli, its utility in bacteria other than E. coli has been hindered by the lack of universal, high-efficiency methods for its implementation and optimization. To address this limitation, we introduce a modular, extensible platform for the generalizable implementation and optimization of GCE in phylogenetically diverse bacteria, based on the host-agnostic serine recombinase-assisted genome engineering toolkit. We apply this approach to five bacterial species and demonstrate robust incorporation of structurally diverse noncanonical amino acids, including a key bacterial post-translational modification. This work provides a generalizable and scalable strategy to deploy expanded genetic systems in bacteria, advancing programmable microbial engineering across diverse applications.IMPORTANCEExpanding the genetic code allows scientists to introduce new chemical functionalities into proteins, creating powerful opportunities to study and engineer biological systems. However, these technologies have remained largely confined to the laboratory bacterium Escherichia coli because adapting them to other bacterial species has been slow and organism-specific. We developed a general, chromosomally integrated framework that makes it easier to establish and optimize genetic code expansion across diverse bacteria. Using this approach, we identify practical design principles for improving performance, demonstrate transferability between distantly related species, and enable site-specific incorporation of modified amino acids into native bacterial proteins. This work expands access to advanced protein engineering technologies for studying bacterial post-translational regulation and developing engineered microbes for biotechnology, environmental applications, and synthetic biology.

mBio.title: TgDDP is a novel DIX domain protein that plays an essential role in Toxoplasma endodyogeny.
mBio.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Apicomplexan parasites are protozoan pathogens responsible for major human diseases, including toxoplasmosis, malaria, and cryptosporidiosis. Toxoplasma gondii has emerged as a model for studying cell division in tissue coccidians. Unlike higher eukaryotes that divide by binary fission, Toxoplasma replicates via internal budding (endodyogeny), yet many factors governing daughter cell biogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize TgDDP (T. gondii DIX-DnaJ domain protein), a previously unannotated protein containing both DIX and DnaJ domains-a unique combination restricted to stramenopiles and apicomplexans. Endogenous tagging revealed that DDP is constitutively expressed and localizes predominantly to the trans-Golgi network in extracellular parasites, with a more dispersed distribution in intravacuolar stages. To assess function, we generated a conditional knockdown line using the auxin-inducible degron system. DDP depletion resulted in a complete block in parasite replication, demonstrating its essential role in the lytic cycle. Microscopy analyses showed that loss of DDP disrupts daughter cell scaffold formation, while nuclear division remains largely intact, indicating a specific role after karyokinesis. Complementation with a wild-type TgDDP allele fully restored parasite replication, and orthologs from related apicomplexans functionally substituted for DDP. Biochemical analysis (SEC-MALS) demonstrated that DDP forms dimers, consistent with DIX domain-containing proteins. Interactome profiling further identified associations with trafficking-related proteins, including clathrins. Together, these findings establish DDP as a critical regulator of daughter cell formation and a potential therapeutic target to inhibit parasite propagation. [IMPORTANCE] Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan parasite that can cause life-threatening disease in humans with immunodeficiency conditions; hence, identifying key factors required for parasite propagation is important to develop novel therapeutics. In this study, we characterize a novel DIX domain-containing protein, DDP, expressed in Toxoplasma. We show that DDP mostly localizes to the trans-Golgi network in extracellular stages and exhibits dispersed localization in the intracellular form. To determine the function of DDP, we generated a conditional knockdown strain and showed that loss of this protein results in abrogation of parasite division. Specifically, parasites lacking DDP are unable to form daughter parasites. Further, the DDP interactome includes trafficking proteins clathrins, along with IMC proteins, thus suggesting that DDP plays an essential role in building daughter cells during endodyogeny.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Decreasing peptide deformylase activity is a beneficial strategy for increasing formaldehyde resistance in Methylobacterium extorquens.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Formaldehyde is a highly toxic metabolite that can cause extensive damage to DNA and proteins, and strategies to mitigate formaldehyde toxicity are poorly understood. Methylotrophic bacteria, such as Methylobacterium extorquens, thrive on one-carbon compounds as sole sources of carbon and energy. These organisms are excellent models for discovering formaldehyde stress response systems because formaldehyde is an obligate intermediate in their central carbon metabolism. Here, we characterize an evolved def allele (defevo) that increases formaldehyde resistance in M. extorquens. The def gene encodes peptide deformylase (PDF, EC:3.5.1.88), an enzyme that contributes to protein processing by removing the formyl group from N-formylmethionine (fMet) on nascent peptides. The defevo allele has a single missense mutation that decreases PDF activity both in vitro and in vivo. Transcriptomic analysis of the defevo strain indicates that there are pleiotropic effects of this mutation and a differential response to formaldehyde stress. We investigate possible mechanisms for the defevo mutant's increased resistance to formaldehyde, including mitigation of formaldehyde-induced protein stress, and altered membrane physiology. We find that the defevo allele selectively alleviates exogenous, but not endogenous, formaldehyde stress, and identify a trade-off in heat shock resistance. This study reports the first observation of lowered PDF activity benefiting a cellular physiological phenotype. Our work indicates that altered protein metabolism can mitigate the toxic effects of formaldehyde and further our understanding of the strategies that protect cells from formaldehyde-induced damage.IMPORTANCEFormaldehyde is a toxic chemical that can damage essential molecules inside of cells, yet all organisms inevitably produce it during normal metabolism. Despite its ubiquity, our understanding of strategies for how cells navigate formaldehyde toxicity is incomplete. This study focuses on Methylobacterium extorquens, which naturally generates high levels of formaldehyde as part of its growth on simple carbon compounds. We show herein that a single genetic change that slows the processing of newly synthesized proteins during translation can unexpectedly improve the bacterium's ability to resist formaldehyde stress. Further, we show that this single change has numerous effects on the cell, many of which may contribute to formaldehyde resistance.

Current Biology.title: Volatile emission dynamics are temporally associated with neighbor-modulated movement in climbing plants
authors: Bianca Bonato, Valentina Simonetti, Sara Avesani, Silvia Guerra, Gabriela Gjinaj, Laura Ravazzolo, Marco Dadda, Umberto Castiello
Current Biology.abstract: Bonato et al. combine three-dimensional kinematic tracking, real-time volatilomic profiling, wavelet coherence, and morphological analyses to investigate plant-plant interactions. In neighboring pea plants, volatile features increase before peak circumnutation velocity, while paired plants show enhanced temporal coordination, revealing a temporal association between chemical dynamics and exploratory movement.

Current Biology.title: The “dark magic mushroom” co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin
authors: Andrew R. Kunik, Michael W. Christopher, Benjamin Lemmond, Bryn T.M. Dentinger, Jason C. Slot, Timothy J. Garrett, Matthew E. Smith
Current Biology.abstract: Kunik et al. discover that a little brown mushroom found in Florida’s swamps co-produces the psychedelic compounds of “magic mushrooms” and amatoxins like those found in the world’s deadliest mushrooms. Evolutionary analyses suggest that the psychedelic genes were acquired via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi rather than passed down.

Current Biology.title: Lateral orbitofrontal cortex enables new learning to overwrite previously acquired information
authors: Maedeh Mahmoudi, Joanne M. Gladding, Michael D. Kendig, Alessandro Castorina, Karly M. Turner, Octavia Soegyono, Laura A. Bradfield
Current Biology.abstract: Mahmoudi et al. show here that contingency degradation is resistant to spontaneous recovery and reinstatement and that its learning, but not retrieval, depends on the lateral orbitofrontal cortex. Together, these findings suggest that unlike extinction, degradation overwrites initial learning and offers a potential approach to the development of relapse-resistant treatments.

Cell Reports.title: The fungal phosphate starvation regulator CtPHO4 couples nutrient adaptation to host colonization through the effector NFC1
authors: Jacy Newfeld, Seishiro Aoki, Hiromi Haba, Momoko Takagi, Nozomu Takahashi, Akane Kubota, Motomu Endo, Kei Hiruma
Cell Reports.abstract: Newfeld et al. identified a fungal effector NFC1 that is necessary for root colonization and host circadian clock perturbation by the conditional plant pathogen C. tofieldiae. NFC1 is tightly suppressed under phosphate deficiency by the fungal transcription factor CtPHO4, showcasing the crucial role of CtPHO4 in balancing virulence with growth.

mSphere.title: A case for interactive visualizations in scientific journals.
mSphere.abstract: Biological data sets are becoming increasingly large, and their complexity often exceeds what static figures can convey. Interactive visualizations offer a way for readers to explore results beyond a single snapshot. Sayegh et al. illustrate this approach by including interactive figures to display results from a large phenotypic screen of Streptococcus pneumoniae growth across 190 carbon sources (F. M. Sayegh, C. Scott, K. Ochoa, et al., mSphere e00460-26, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1128/msphere.00460-26). We argue that although such visualizations are increasingly straightforward to build, the barrier to their broader adoption is no longer technical but editorial, and integrating them directly into online articles would meaningfully advance how complex data sets are communicated.

mSphere.title: Carbon source-dependent growth heterogeneity across Streptococcus pneumoniae serotypes revealed through interactive data visualization.
mSphere.abstract: Bacteria at the host-pathogen interface must continuously adapt their metabolism to the nutrient landscape of the host environment. More than 30% of the Streptococcus pneumoniae genome is dedicated to carbohydrate transport and metabolism, thus underscoring the importance of central carbon metabolism in host adaptation and survival. Despite this, comprehensive comparisons of carbon source-dependent growth dynamics across diverse pneumococcal serotypes remain limited. In this study, we used Biolog phenotype microarray plates together with a physiologically relevant defined medium, RPMI 1640, to characterize carbon source utilization and growth phenotypes across encapsulated serotypes and non-encapsulated strains. While several carbon sources supported conserved growth patterns across serotypes or strains, substantial serotype-specific variation was observed in carbon source utilization, maximal growth achieved, growth kinetics, and the timing of the death phase or the extent of autolysis. To address limitations in conventional data presentation, we present an interactive visualization framework for bacterial growth analysis. In the web version of this article, readers can dynamically explore carbon source-dependent phenotypes through interactive heatmaps linked to full growth curves, enabling detailed examination of growth phases, kinetic transitions, and autolysis events, alongside Venn diagrams that highlight serotype- and carbon source-specific phenotypic differences. The underlying code is publicly available via GitHub, providing a template for interactive data exploration. Together, these findings provide a valuable resource for investigating pneumococcal metabolic adaptation in host-relevant nutrient environments and demonstrate how interactive publication can enhance exploration and interpretation of complex bacterial growth data sets. IMPORTANCE As bacteria adapt their metabolism to nutritional environments, comprehensive comparisons across experimental data sets are often limited by their scale and complexity. Here, we characterize carbon source utilization across Streptococcus pneumoniae serotypes and strains, revealing both conserved and strain-specific growth dynamics that likely contribute to colonization and disease potential. We also address a broader challenge: how large, high-dimensional data sets are presented and interpreted in peer-reviewed publications. Current figures compress multidimensional kinetic data into single, static representations, limiting a reader's ability to independently evaluate the underlying dynamics. To overcome this limitation, we developed an interactive data visualization platform directly into the web-based article, enabling readers to explore the data while maintaining full data transparency. This approach advances data presentation in peer-reviewed research by providing a generalizable framework to improve the accessibility, interpretability, and evaluation of complex biological data sets.

mSphere.title: Genetic detoxification of an unencapsulated Neisseria meningitidis strain enhances potency of outer membrane vesicle vaccines and cross-reactivity of vaccine-specific antibodies.
mSphere.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Meningococcal serogroup B (MenB) detergent-detoxified outer membrane vesicle (dOMV) vaccines demonstrate high effectiveness against the homologous production strain but confer limited cross-protection to heterologous strains. We previously reported that dOMVs isolated from a MenB strain deleted for the proteins PorA, PorB, and RmpM (ΔABR) elicited bactericidal antibodies with a greater breadth of coverage, but of lower overall titer, compared to wild-type (WT) dOMV-induced antibodies. Low ΔABR dOMV potency was associated with pronounced vesicular deterioration and lower levels of lipooligosaccharide (LOS) and capsular polysaccharide (Cps) relative to WT dOMVs, phenotypes resulting from detergent detoxification procedures required to limit LOS-induced toxicity. In this study, we engineered genetically detoxified ΔABR strains that were deleted singly for the lauroyl acyltransferase LpxL1 (ΔABRL) or in tandem for the Cps polysialyltransferase SiaD (ΔABRSL). Genetically detoxified, detergent-extracted OMVs (eOMVs) from ΔABRL and ΔABRSL retained vesicular structure and elicited functional antibodies with increased cross-reactivity compared to ΔABR and ΔABRL dOMVs when administered to rabbits. Antibody seropositivity and cross-reactivity were similarly increased in mice vaccinated with ΔABRL eOMVs vs ΔABRL dOMVs. ΔABRSL eOMV potency was higher than that of ΔABRL eOMVs, suggesting a role for Cps in suppressing antibody responses. Immunization with eOMVs was associated with trends toward improved murine T helper cell responses and elicitation of higher proportions of conformational antibodies that may have contributed to improved bactericidal activity. ΔABRSL eOMVs additionally showed decreased toxicity compared to WT and ΔABR dOMVs when tested in vitro, supporting further study as a vaccine candidate. [IMPORTANCE] The ability to target multiple serogroup B Neisseria meningitidis strains with a single vesicle vaccine is complicated by the diversity of antigens that span the bacterial surface. We previously reported that vesicles isolated from meningococcal strains deleted for the major antigenically diverse surface proteins elicited functional antibodies that could kill a large number of N. meningitidis strains though at relatively low titers. Low potency of the mutant vaccines was associated with a breakdown of the vesicular membrane upon detergent treatment, a process necessary to diminish endogenous endotoxin levels and ensure vaccine safety. In this study, we demonstrate that we can retain high cross-reactivity of anti-vesicle antibodies without decreasing the potency of the host immune response through genetic detoxification of the meningococcal vaccine strain. By preventing the formation of the complete endotoxin structure, we are able to isolate vesicles that are safe and immunogenic without the requirement for detergent detoxification.

Biogeosciences.title: Plant hydraulic traits regulating productivity and drought resistance in boreal crops
Biogeosciences.abstract: Plant hydraulic traits regulating productivity and drought resistance in boreal crops Hui Tang, Samuli Launiainen, Julius Vira, Liisa Kulmala, Taru Palosuo, Hermanni Aaltonen, Olli Nevalainen, Istem Fer, Henriikka Vekuri, Jari-Pekka Nousu, Mika Korkiakoski, and Jari Liski Biogeosciences, 23, 8183–8205, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8183-2026, 2026 How do crops in northern regions cope with drought? We combined several years of field measurements with computer simulations to study oats and forage grasses in Finland. Both crops used water cautiously, helping preserve soil moisture and sustain growth during dry periods. However, dry air limited their growth more strongly than dry soil. These findings can help improve predictions of crop performance and support farming as drought risks increase in northern regions.

Biogeosciences.title: Multi-centennial ocean biogeochemical responses to extended Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
Biogeosciences.abstract: Multi-centennial ocean biogeochemical responses to extended Shared Socioeconomic Pathways Hidetaka Kobayashi, Tokuta Yokohata, Akitomo Yamamoto, Tomohiro Hajima, Hiroaki Tatebe, Akira Oka, and Keith B. Rodgers Biogeosciences, 23, 7807–7847, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-7807-2026, 2026 Using long-term MIROC-ES2L simulations under extended Shared Socio-economic Pathway (SSP) scenarios to 2500, we show that ocean–atmosphere pCO2 disequilibrium exhibits strong scenario dependence. Low emissions lead to near equilibrium by 2100, whereas high emissions drive expanding oceanic CO2 supersaturation and declining buffering capacity. Marine ecosystem stress persists for centuries, reflecting the ocean’s long memory and limited reversibility.

Biogeosciences.abstract: Organic matter composition and origin differ between restored and natural UK saltmarshes up to 100 years after the breach Catrina Gore, Peter Mueller, Mark Chapman, Franck Dal Molin, Gerhard Schmiedl, Yvonne Milker, Lisa Benson, Alina Marca, and Stefanie Nolte Biogeosciences, 23, 8207–8231, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8207-2026, 2026 Various chemical and physical analyses were performed with mud samples from four restored UK saltmarshes to determine the origin of the organic matter (OM) present. The plants growing on the marsh could have supplied the OM or it could have been washed in by the tides from other ecosystems. In the restored marshes much of the OM came from the latter source and by making comparisons with existing data from natural saltmarshes, it was determined that this was not true of these sites.

Smith, Alexandra G. Konings, Martin J. Baur, Marvin Browne, David Chaparro, Charles Devine, Jen L. Diehl, Arthur Endsley, Thomas Jagdhuber, Kristine M. Biogeosciences.title: CO2 fertilization to climate limitation: shifting drivers in a dryland forest
Biogeosciences.abstract: CO2 fertilization to climate limitation: shifting drivers in a dryland forest Katja Irob, Liling Chang, Yakir Preisler, Sebastian Fiedler, Matthias Büchner, José M. Grünzweig, and Efrat Sheffer Biogeosciences, 23, 8097–8116, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8097-2026, 2026 Dryland forests are promoted for climate mitigation, but their persistence under future climate is uncertain. Using a calibrated forest model and 21 years of field data from an arid pine forest, we simulated carbon uptake and growth through 2100. Rising carbon dioxide initially boosted productivity, but compound drought and heat stress later overrode these benefits. Lovenduski, Dimitris Menemenlis, and Hong Zhang Biogeosciences, 23, 8063–8077, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8063-2026, 2026 The ocean helps slow climate change by absorbing carbon dioxide, but our research shows this process weakens quickly when we reduce emissions. Biogeosciences.abstract: Frequent resuspension of glaciomarine coastal sediments as an important source of iron to the West Antarctic Peninsula Rhiannon L. Jones, Maeve C. Lohan, Tobias Ehmen, Lisa Friberg, Ben Lincoln, Katy Sheen, Siobhán Foden, Katrien Van Landeghem, Kate Retallick, George Dadd, James Scourse, and Amber L. Annett Biogeosciences, 23, 8117–8135, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8117-2026, 2026 In the ocean, iron is an essential yet scarce nutrient for primary producers. Melting glaciers in the Antarctic deliver high amounts of sediment, rich in iron, to the coastal seafloor. This study investigates the reactivity and magnitude of iron released when seafloor sediment is resuspended into the water column by tidal and wave processes. These sediments are highly reactive and release high amounts of iron. We suggest these coastal processes are key for supplying iron to the Antarctic shelf.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Pepti-DrugPhAI: Multimodal AI-evaluator for functional pharmacokinetics and toxicity of peptides
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Elizaveta A. Bogdanova, Timofei F. Lukianov, Artem V. Chernukhin, Alexey K. Shaytan Peptide drugs exhibit exceptional selectivity for biological targets and high functional activity making them among the most promising therapeutic agents. However, unsatisfactory pharmacokinetic characteristics remain a critical barrier to their implementation. They often become the primary reason for the failure of promising candidates in preclinical and clinical trials. To address this issue, we present Pepti-DrugPhAI – a comprehensive algorithm for the precise prediction of the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of a wide range of peptide compounds. Unlike many existing solutions, the proposed algorithm is multimodal and can simultaneously process both SMILES representations of chemical structures and amino acid sequences. This ensures efficient processing not only of canonical peptides but also of non-canonical modifications, cyclic structures, and peptide-like small molecules. We also created an original dataset for model training integrating data from public databases and relevant scientific publications. The algorithm simultaneously predicts key parameters including membrane permeability (Caco-2 and PAMPA penetration), distribution and excretion (half-life, clearance, volume of distribution), as well as general and specific toxicity profiles (neurotoxicity, hemolytic activity). A key innovation of the study is the integration of functional pharmacokinetic scoring. The model not only predicts ADMET values but also calculates an adaptive suitability rating for a compound in the context of its specific biological activity. We have conducted a comparative analysis of various data encoding strategies implementing a stack of models ranging from classical machine learning methods to modern transformers and language models in classification modes. Results from testing on independent test sets demonstrate high prediction accuracy and interpretability of features making Pepti-DrugPhAI a powerful tool for more robust selection of promising peptide drug candidates. All data and the code are available in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/EABogdanova/Pepti-DrugPhAI.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Sphinx: An R package for adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis in spatial omics
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Mengyi Yan, Xiaoxiu Tan, Zhenhao Liu, Siwen Zhang, Yiwen Du, Hong Li, Lanming Chen, Lu Xie Spatial omics enables analysis of tissue microenvironmental heterogeneity, but most spatial tools are optimized for transcriptomics and poorly suited to proteomics data. We developed Sphinx, an R package providing a comprehensive workflow for spatial proteomics, including preprocessing, cell annotation, adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling, and functional characterization. Importantly, it introduces an adaptive parameter selection framework guided by spatial statistical metrics and incorporates computational optimizations for large-scale datasets, enabling robust neighborhood modeling. Notably, Sphinx offers improved computational efficiency and scalability. Across lung adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, and mouse spleen datasets, Sphinx robustly identifies cell types and spatial functional units, including tertiary lymphoid structures. We also explored the application of Sphinx to paired high-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets, illustrating its potential applicability. Sphinx provides a flexible and efficient framework for spatial proteomics, enabling robust characterization of spatial organization and tissue microenvironments.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Burst-to-burst information resetting in sequential rhythmic neural activity
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Pablo Sanchez-Martin, Irene Elices, Alicia Garrido-Peña, Carlos Garcia-Saura, Rafael Levi, Francisco B. Rodriguez, Pablo Varona In multiple neural systems, networks of bursting neurons generate and coordinate robust sequential rhythms, such as those observed in central pattern generators (CPGs) that control motor activity. In this paper, we combine electrophysiological experiments and biophysical models of the pyloric CPG to investigate cycle-by-cycle coordination resetting in sequential rhythms. In particular, we focus our analysis on the variability constraints of sequence intervals defined by the burst onset and offset time references, which structure the timing of the rhythmic CPG sequence cycle-by-cycle. We identified the conditions under which sequential dynamical invariants emerge as robust relationships between specific intervals within the same cycle, and when such relations reset at each cycle or extend between intervals of consecutive cycles. Our results help understand the mechanisms underlying the autonomous cycle-by-cycle sequential coordination and the relationships between intervals from consecutive cycles when a slow modulatory action establishes a common trend across the rhythm.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: An antigen-specific protein language model guides CDR optimization for antibody design
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Faisal Bin Ashraf, Karen Paco, Sanaz Zebardast, Zihao Zhang, Ryan Mooney, Christian J. Dávila Ojeda, Mariana Paco Mendivil, Rashid M. Alam, Eva Chen, Iraneus Ogu, Jordan A. Lay, Tristan Y. Yang, Fernando L. Barroso da Silva, Malkiat Johal, Ilya Tolstorukov, Matthew H. Sazinsky, Animesh Ray, Stefano Lonardi The capacity of an antibody to recognize and bind an antigen with high specificity and strength (i.e., its binding affinity) is a key determinant in the design and optimization of neutralizing antibodies against pathogenic targets. Here we introduce Ab-Affinity, a fine-tuned protein language model (PLM) that predicts the binding affinity of an antibody against a target peptide within the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. Cross-validation results shows that that Ab-Affinity outperforms other PLM-based affinity predictors when evaluated on a held-out validation and independent test sets. When integrated with a genetic algorithm and simulated annealing for sequence diversification and fitness optimization, Ab-Affinity enables the generation of candidate antibodies exhibiting over 100-fold improvement in predicted binding affinity relative to its parental (natural) antibody. More broadly, antibodies designed with Ab-Affinity attain higher predicted binding affinities than those produced by alternative mutational strategies, yielding synthetic antibodies with favorable predicted biophysical characteristics. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations for the strongest synthetic candidates indicate enhanced interactions and increased stability with the target peptide epitope within the spike protein. Experimental validation in vitro for a top-ranked candidate reveals an apparent increase in binding relative to its parental antibody. All model weights, source code, and analysis pipelines are publicly released to allow full reproducibility.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: PhysInfer: A physics-constrained neural network for adaptive inference of transcriptional bursting from single-cell RNA-seq
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Xiaodong Zeng, Jingwen Zhang, Shan Li, Haohua Wang Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has established that gene expression is driven by stochastic transcriptional bursting. However, inferring burst dynamics from static scRNA-seq snapshots is fundamentally constrained by parameter unidentifiability and model topology mismatch. Here, we propose PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that integrates a physics-constrained neural network with adaptive model selection and parameter decoupling. A physics-informed loss function, combining stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring, reparameterizes the optimization from unidentifiable microscopic rates to an interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representation of burst size and burst frequency, thereby providing an interpretable parameterization for assessing practical recoverability in static data. Validation on synthetic data with known ground-truth parameters confirms high inference accuracy in low-to-medium activation regimes and shows that recovery of BS and productive BF becomes increasingly condition-dependent as the ON-state probability approaches saturation; under different recovery criteria, the condition-specific upper Pon limit for simultaneously recovering BS and productive BF varies with cell number and capture efficiency. Applied to a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) dataset, PhysInfer reconstructs a transcriptional dynamic manifold across the 2,137-gene secondary BIC analysis set, showing cross-gene variation in fitted burst frequency and burst size. A model-specific stationary likelihood combined with zero-count anchoring improves robustness to zero-heavy observations. The adaptive topology module further identifies a distinct subset of genes with stable support for an effective sequential 3-state representation, revealing distributional structure beyond that captured by standard 2-state fitting. PhysInfer thus provides a robust, topology-adaptive, and interpretable solution for characterizing transcriptional kinetic patterns from static single-cell transcriptomic snapshots.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Sebastian Manuel Geli, Juan Manuel Monti, Adrián Ponce-Alvarez, Gustavo Deco, Yonatan Sanz Perl A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region’s future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation–dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain’s memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: MethMarkerDB 2.0: an expanded and functionally annotated database for cancer DNA methylation biomarkers.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Cancer-associated differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are promising biomarkers for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic response, but their biological significance and potential applications remain to be systematically explored across datasets. To support this, we released MethMarkerDB 2.0 (https://methmarkerdb.hzau.edu.cn/v2), which provides several improvements over the previous version: (i) Expands the data resource from 13 to 21 cancer types and from 658 to 1236 whole-genome methylome samples, comprising ∼5.6 million candidate DMRs and 6411 literature-curated biomarker records.(ii) Integrates 450K DNA methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Epigenome-Wide Association Study Atlas and transcript annotations into the "MethMarker Gene Search" module. These data provide complementary evidence from independent datasets and platforms and allow users to examine CpG-level information for individual DMRs. Additionally, cell-type-resolved reference methylation data allow users to check cellular-background methylation. (iii) Introduces four analysis modules to characterize DMR methylation patterns across age groups and spatial ecotypes, and connect DMRs with transcription factor binding evidence and cancer cell-line drug responses. Moreover, the "Methylation-Cas Designer" supports guide RNA design for methylation-sensitive restriction enzyme-Cas assays and targeted epigenome editing. In summary, MethMarkerDB 2.0 provides expanded resources, diverse functional analyses, and experimental design tools, facilitating the interpretation and application of cancer-associated DMRs.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: MobiDB in 2027: machine-actionable access to intrinsic protein disorder knowledge.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: MobiDB (https://mobidb.org) integrates structural and functional annotations for intrinsically disordered proteins and regions across UniProtKB. The 2027 release strengthens semantic consistency, programmatic access, and reproducible reuse. A refined controlled vocabulary groups features in a hierarchical way and distinguishes evidence classes and types annotation sources as providers, methods, or aggregation rules. A new versioned REST API, along with a developed MCP server, enables scripts, workflows, and tool-using artificial intelligence systems to retrieve and combine evidence-bearing records through documented operations. The redesigned website applies the same vocabulary to protein entries, documentation, and cross-proteome statistics. Additional developments include standardized Nextflow production workflows, updated RING Protein Data Bank interaction processing, integration of Motif Map of the Proteome and Linear Motif mediated Protein-Protein Interaction Database annotations, and a release-aware catalogue of static datasets for large-scale analysis. Following the recent increase in reference proteomes in UniProtKB, MobiDB now provides a more representative estimate of long-disorder with a median residue coverage of 12.3% in eukaryotes, 1.9% in archaea, 1.7% in bacteria, and 3.4% in viruses; and protein prevalence of 48.7%, 11.9%, 11.2%, and 25.0%, respectively. Together, these developments make disorder knowledge easier to discover, relate to function, and reuse with explicit provenance.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: oRNAment V2: an expanded database of putative RNA binding protein target sites in the transcriptomes of diverse model species.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) modulate the expression, form, and fate of RNA transcripts throughout their lifecycle, thereby serving as essential regulators of gene expression. Despite impactful high-throughput experimental advances that have enabled in vitro and in vivo identification of RBP binding sites, few resources provide a comprehensive catalog of potential RBP binding sites transcriptome-wide. To address this limitation, we previously developed oRNAment, a database of putative RBP binding sites across coding and non-coding transcriptome regions in human and four model species. Here, we present oRNAment V2, a significantly enhanced resource, with an expanded collection of RBPs, motifs, species, and the addition of intronic sequences. The updated oRNAment resource now predicts a total of 3 808 264 959 putative RBP binding sites across the transcriptomes of human and 14 species. Novel features of oRNAment include predictions of binding site evolutionary age, annotations of CLIP support, and visualizations with UCSC track hubs for all putative RBP binding sites. On the front end, oRNAment's web interface enhances functionality and usability by providing improved search and filtering functions, download options, and visualizations. With its expansion, oRNAment V2 continues to provide an important resource to support research by the RNA community. oRNAment V2 is available at https://rnabiology.ircm.qc.ca/oRNAmentv2.

eLife.title: Engineering ATP import in yeast uncovers a synthetic route to extend cellular lifespan
eLife.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction and declining ATP production are common features of aging, yet whether ATP availability itself directly regulates cellular lifespan is unclear. However, the causal relationship between cellular ATP homeostasis and aging has not been established. Here, we developed a synthetic system to manipulate intracellular ATP independently of endogenous energy production by expressing a plasma membrane-targeted nucleotide transporter, NTT1, from the intracellular parasite Encephalitozoon cuniculi in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. NTT1 expression depleted intracellular ATP in the absence of extracellular ATP, whereas ATP supplementation produced robust NTT1-dependent ATP uptake, and increased intracellular ATP abundance. ATP availability strongly influenced replicative lifespan: ATP depletion shortened lifespan, whereas ATP supplementation restored and extended lifespan in NTT1-expressing cells. Unexpectedly, extracellular ATP also extended lifespan in wild-type cells that lack ATP import, revealing an NTT1-independent response to extracellular ATP. Transcriptomic analyses showed that NTT1-mediated ATP import suppresses glucose uptake, carbohydrate catabolism, mitochondrial respiration, and autophagy, whereas extracellular ATP elicits a distinct transcriptional response in wild-type cells involving metabolic, mitochondrial, and signaling pathways. Single-cell aging analyses further showed that ATP supplementation extends lifespan across distinct aging trajectories and shifts cells away from the mitochondrial dysfunction-associated aging state. Finally, experiments in cells lacking mitochondrial DNA separated these effects mechanistically: NTT1-associated lifespan phenotypes and high-ATP toxicity required functional mitochondria, whereas extracellular ATP extended lifespan in wild-type cells independently of mitochondrial respiration. Together, these findings demonstrate that ATP availability is a direct regulator of cellular aging and reveal distinct metabolic and extracellular ATP-responsive routes through which cellular energy state influences longevity.

eLife.title: Cholinergic blockade reveals a role for human hippocampal theta in memory encoding but not retrieval
eLife.abstract: Cholinergic dysfunction is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease and other memory disorders. Yet, the neurophysiological mechanisms linking cholinergic signaling to memory remain poorly understood. In this study, we administered scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, to neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes as they performed an associative recognition memory task. When scopolamine was present at encoding, we observed disruptions to hippocampal slow theta oscillations (2–4 Hz), with selective impairments to recollection-based memory. However, when scopolamine was present during retrieval alone, we observed disruptions to slow theta without impaired memory performance. These disruptions included dose-dependent reductions in theta power, theta phase reset, and encoding–retrieval pattern reinstatement. Together, our results challenge the notion that theta oscillations are necessary for memory retrieval, and instead suggest that theta universally reflects an encoding-related neural state. These findings motivate updates to current models of acetylcholine’s role in memory and may inform future therapies targeting rhythmic biomarkers of memory dysfunction.

eLife.title: Multimodal single-cell analyses reveal distinct fusion-regulated transcriptional programs in Ewing sarcoma
eLife.abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a fusion-driven malignancy, peaking in adolescence. Although EwS tumors are driven uniquely by EWS::FLI1 and related fusions, patient outcomes vary greatly. If and how tumor plasticity of EWS::FLI1-regulated transcriptional signatures contributes to disease progression is not known. To address this, we utilized a single-cell co-assay of RNA and chromatin accessibility (ATAC) sequencing to identify gene regulatory networks in EwS. By comprehensively characterizing regulatory elements across cell lines, we identified multiple unique modules of gene regulation. Differential usage and prevalence of these modules was evident across cell lines, associated with distinct epigenetic and transcriptomic signatures, and in specific cases, modifiable by exogenous TGF-β. When we examined primary EwS patient tumors, we observed these same regulatory modules were variably enriched both across and within tumors, highlighting the existence of intratumoral heterogeneity in gene regulatory networks. Our findings demonstrate that multiple, co-existing transcriptional programs shape the phenotypic diversity of EwS and suggest that the balance between these networks may have important implications for clinical outcomes and targeted therapy development.

PLOS Biology.title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Theresa M. Pauli, Theresa von Heyl, Beate Rieblinger, Sabrina Teresa Schleibinger, Wei Liang, Antonia Schmauser, Mithuoshni Arullmoli, Paul Derrer, Anika Eckstein, Sirradu Jagana, Camila Gatti Corrêa, Krzysztof Flisikowski, Tatiana Flisikowska, Benjamin Schusser Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human–animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

PLOS Biology.title: The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry sequentially drives invasion and host-parasite interface formation
PLOS Biology.abstract: by Allison Cohen, Tim Bergner, Amandine Guérin, Maryse Lebrun, Michael Laue, Christian Klotz, Boris Striepen The apicomplexan parasite Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease in young children. Within the intestinal epithelium, Cryptosporidium establishes a unique intracellular niche in the apical brush border of enterocytes. A structurally complex interface between host and parasite acts as a holdfast and enables protein and metabolite transport. How the parasite invades its host cell and builds the interface is poorly understood. Here, we reveal parasite invasion with high temporal and spatial resolution using rigorous molecular markers. We find that sequential discharge of specialized secretory organelles anchors the parasite within the host prior to internalization. The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry persists beyond its initial pre-invasion discharge, acting as a conduit for the secretion of multiple waves of effector proteins. Ultimately, the rhoptry membrane gives rise to the feeder organelle that separates host from parasite cytoplasm. These findings lead us to propose a mechanistic model of Cryptosporidium invasion and intracellular parasitism.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Integrated physiological and multiomic analyses reveal the multilayered aluminum tolerance mechanisms of acidophilic alga Coccomyxa sp. A2.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Acid mine drainage (AMD) is a pervasive global environmental challenge, and algal-based bioremediation represents one of the most robust strategies for its treatment. However, the mechanisms by which algae survive in metal-rich AMD remain largely unclear. Here, we integrated physiological, transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses to explore the tolerance mechanisms of the acidophilic alga Coccomyxa sp. A2 to aluminum (Al), a metal prevalent in AMD. The results demonstrated that A2 exhibited substantially higher Al tolerance than the model alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii under their respective optimal pH conditions. Upon Al exposure, A2 significantly increased the extracellular levels of three strong organic acids (oxalic, citric, and tartaric acids), thereby facilitating chelation of free Al3+ present in the acidic environment. In the near-neutral cytosol, A2 accumulated a broader array of organic acids at higher concentrations to sequester Al despite severe extracellular H+ stress. To restrict Al influx, A2 enhanced the synthesis of cellulose, hemicellulose, and proteins across the distinct layers of its cell wall, increasing cell wall dry weight by 66%. This remodeling was probably supported by starch degradation, enhanced gluconeogenesis, and Calvin cycle activation, which together supplied sufficient monosaccharide precursors for polysaccharide synthesis. Concurrently, the upregulation of glycosyltransferases facilitated rapid polysaccharide chain elongation. To scavenge ROS, the alga likely initiated a temporally coordinated, biphasic antioxidant response, in which non-enzymatic ascorbic acid pools compensated for lagging superoxide dismutase activity during the early acute phase of stress. Calcium, abscisic acid, and jasmonic acid coordinated these defense mechanisms, with calcium serving as the primary signaling hub.IMPORTANCEThe conventional treatment method for acid mine drainage (AMD) involves neutralization with lime, which is costly and generates large amounts of sludge that is difficult to manage. The application of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) presents a promising alternative by eliminating secondary pollution and enabling metal sulfide recovery. However, a key challenge of this approach is ensuring an affordable and sustainable organic carbon source for SRB since AMD is oligotrophic. A potential solution is the in-situ cultivation of acidophilic algae. Given the high metal concentrations in AMD, investigating the metal tolerance mechanisms of acidophilic algae is vital for producing sufficient biomass to support SRB. Meanwhile, about 40% of the world's arable soils are acidic, and these soils typically contain high concentrations of aluminum (Al), which is a major factor limiting crop production. Therefore, research on the exceptional Al tolerance mechanisms of acidophilic algae can provide insights into improving crop metal resistance through genetic engineering techniques.

Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Temperature defines metabolic states that lead to seasonal adaptation of the soil nitrite oxidizer Nitrobacter vulgaris strain CN101.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) play a central role in nitrification, yet their temperature-dependent ecophysiology remains poorly understood, particularly in terrestrial environments. In this study, the physiological and transcriptomic responses of Nitrobacter vulgaris strain CN101, isolated from forest soil in Japan, were investigated across different culture temperatures. Temperature-dependent kinetics revealed two distinct activation energies below and above 20°C, suggesting a shift in metabolic state. At lower temperatures, nitrite oxidation rates declined, and transcriptomic analysis showed reduced expression of genes involved in electron transport and protein synthesis, whereas genes related to carbon and nitrogen assimilation remained relatively unchanged. Electron microscopy revealed smaller cell size and simplified membrane structures under low-temperature conditions. Together, these findings indicate that metabolic activity is maintained while biomass production is constrained below 20°C. At higher temperatures, efficient electron transport, increased translational capacity, and enlarged cell morphology were restored, consistent with a growth-promoting state. These coordinated metabolic and structural changes suggest that strain CN101 adopts a temperature-dependent strategy that balances survival and proliferation in seasonally fluctuating forest soils. By integrating physiological, ultrastructural, and transcriptomic analyses, this study provides a concrete example of how temperature influences the ecophysiological adaptation of terrestrial NOB.IMPORTANCENitrification is a key microbial process in the global nitrogen cycle, yet how nitrifying microorganisms remain active under fluctuating environmental conditions remains poorly understood. In temperate soils, seasonal temperature variation strongly influences nitrification, but the physiological responses of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) remain largely unexplored. In this study, we show that the soil nitrite oxidizer Nitrobacter vulgaris strain CN101 exhibits temperature-dependent physiological states, shifting from a metabolically active but growth-limited state at low temperatures to a state of active growth at higher temperatures. These findings demonstrate how temperature restructures NOB metabolism and physiology. This study provides a representative example of the seasonal ecophysiology of soil nitrifiers and highlights temperature-driven physiological restructuring as a key mechanism shaping nitrification dynamics in terrestrial ecosystems.
